en: The Mahākaruṇā-sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter One: The Brahmā Devas. Chapter One: The Brahmā Devas.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying between the twin śāla trees at the birthplace of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara.
At that time, as the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
“You should prepare a seat between the twin śāla trees; lie down on your right side like a lion king, for I shall enter parinirvāṇa during the latter part of this night.”
Ānanda! I have attained ultimate *parinirvāṇa* and have severed all conditioned discourse.

I have performed the work of a Buddha and have proclaimed the nectar—the dwelling-less, profound, subtle, and wondrous concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), which is difficult to see, difficult to awaken to, and difficult to measure—the noble and holy Dharma known by those of clear wisdom.
I have turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma three times; whether it be any śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, māra, brahmā, or human, none can turn it by means of worldly common dharmas.
I have already beaten the Dharma drum, blown the Dharma conch, raised the Dharma banner, launched the Dharma ship, constructed the Dharma bridge, and let fall the Dharma rain.

I have already illuminated the trichiliocosm with light, extinguishing the great darkness, revealing the right path to sentient beings, and liberating them; I have brought fulfillment and benefit to devas and humans, and all those who were to be delivered have now been delivered.
I have already subdued all non-Buddhists and their various heterodox arguments; I have shaken the palaces of Māra and crushed his power.

Uttering the Great Lion’s Roar, I perform the works of the Buddhas, establish the deeds of a great man, fulfill my original vows, protect and uphold the Eye of the Dharma, instruct the great Śrāvakas, and bestow predictions upon Bodhisattvas, so that the Buddha-eye may not be severed in the future.
"Ānanda! From this day forth, I have nothing further to do; I shall only enter parinirvāṇa.
When Ānanda heard these words, he was pierced by the arrows of grief and became exceedingly distressed. Weeping and shedding tears, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Bhagavān! Nirvāṇa has come too soon.”
"Sugata! Nirvāṇa has come too soon.
The eye of the world is extinguished; the world is left orphaned and without refuge; there is no guide."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"Cease, do not grieve or lament, Ānanda!
It is impossible that dharmas which are born, dharmas which exist, conditioned dharmas, and perishable dharmas should not cease.
I have told you before: all things that are beloved and agreeable must inevitably be separated from us.

Ānanda! You have already served and attended upon me with a mind of loving-kindness, a non-dual mind, and a mind free from malice, as well as through physical deeds of filial support and compliance that were boundless.

Ānanda! If gods, humans, asuras, and others were to serve and make offerings to śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas for less than a kalpa or for a full kalpa, yet were to serve and make offerings to the Tathāgata for even a single moment, their merit would be far greater than that.
Since you have made offerings to the Buddha of Great Supernatural Power up until his parinirvāṇa, you shall obtain great merit and vast virtue.
It is like nectar—the foremost nectar, the final nectar—which is ultimate nirvāṇa.
"Therefore, Ānanda, do not grieve or lament. At that time, Ānanda,
wiping away his tears in sorrow and grief, prepared a seat for the Tathāgata between the twin trees, arranging it according to the manner of the lion’s right-side reclining posture.

Immediately, all the trees, medicinal herbs, and forests within this trichiliocosm turned toward the place where the Tathāgata was entering parinirvāṇa; some were about to fall over, some were bent double, some were about to touch the ground, and some had already fallen to the earth.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the streams within this trichiliocosm—the great rivers, small rivers, springs, pools, and lakes—ceased their flow and remained still.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, all birds and beasts within the trichiliocosm remained silent, neither crying out nor eating.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the suns, moons, stars, planetary bodies, firelight, luminous pearls, and even glowworms within the trichiliocosm failed to appear; they were devoid of radiance and unable to illuminate anything.
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, all the fierce fires within the trichiliocosm were completely extinguished; they did not burn, did not heat, and could not scorch or parch anything.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, all the fierce fires of every hell within the trichiliocosm became entirely cool and refreshing.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, all sentient beings dwelling in those hells attained peace and happiness in an instant.

All animals throughout the trichiliocosm gave rise to hearts of loving-kindness and compassion; they no longer harbored anger or resentment toward one another, nor did they inflict harm or take each other’s lives.
All hungry ghosts were freed from hunger and thirst.

By the Buddha’s spiritual power, all sentient beings experienced exultation in body and mind; they were liberated from suffering and attained tranquility, becoming fully endowed with the supreme bliss that accords with their wishes.

When the World-Honored One lay on his right side, the entire trichiliocosm—including all the Sumeru Kings, the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, Mount Mucilinda, Mount Gandhamādana, Mount Himavat, the various Black Mountains, the great earth, and the vast oceans—trembled in six ways: namely, shaking, surging, rising, quaking, roaring, and awakening.
All the wind-circles throughout the trichiliocosm ceased to stir.

For a single kṣaṇa, all sentient beings abandoned their various activities and dwelt in tranquility; free from sleep, their minds were undistracted, and all desires to act subsided as they remained silent and without sound.

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, all the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Brahmās, Śakras, and World-Protecting Kings within the trichiliocosm each saw their palaces, thrones, and gardens become utterly dim and dark; they no longer possessed majestic radiance, and they felt no more affection or delight. Their retinues were likewise filled with anxiety and distress, finding no joy.
The Brahmā King, Lord of a thousand worlds, and the Great Brahmā King, Lord of a trichiliocosm, being arrogant and self-important, conceived such thoughts and held such views:
"I created this world and all its sentient beings; I transformed them."
Due to the Buddha’s spiritual power, Mahābrahmā, the lord of that trichiliocosm, saw that his own palace, throne, and other furnishings had become dim and lusterless, and he felt no joy in them;
the same was true for Maheśvara, the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, and others as well.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the trichiliocosm, had this thought:
"By whose power has this sign appeared,
causing me to find no pleasure in my palace or my throne?"

At that time, the Great Brahmā King surveyed this trichiliocosm and saw that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—the sovereign lord of wealth and great mastery who had brought about its creation—was to enter parinirvāṇa this very day at the end of the night. For this reason, he manifested these supernatural powers, transformations, inconceivable wonders, and unprecedented events; these supernatural powers were precisely the signs of the Tathāgata’s entry into nirvāṇa.

At that time, after the Great Brahmā King had formed this thought, he became sorrowful and unhappy; trembling with fear, his hair stood on end, and in great haste and agitation, surrounded by the assembly of Brahmās, he went together to the place where the Buddha was.
All the other Brahmā devas in this trichiliocosm had already previously accepted the noble Dharma and were dwelling securely in the noble Dharma.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of the trichiliocosm, having approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and addressed him, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will instruct me as to how I should abide."
"How should one practice?
Having spoken these words, the Tathāgata immediately asked the Great Brahmā King: "Brahmā!..."
Do you now truly harbor such thoughts as these:
"I am Mahābrahmā; I am superior to others and they are not my equal; I am a wise one"?
I am the Great Lord of Sovereignty within this trichiliocosm; I create sentient beings and manifest sentient beings, and I create worlds and manifest worlds.
"Is it not so? The Great Brahmā replied, "It is so, Bhagavān!"
"So it is, Sugata! The Buddha said, "Brahmā!"
"By whom were you created?
By whom were you emanated?
At that time, that Brahmā remained silent.
Seeing that the Brahmā remained silent, the Buddha asked again: "Brahmā!
There are times when this trichiliocosm is consumed by the fires of the kalpa, blazing and glowing with intense heat."
"What do you think?
Was this created by you? Was this emanated by you?
At that time, Mahābrahmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, "Brahmā!
In this way, the great earth rests upon a mass of water; the water rests upon the wind; and the wind rests upon space.
Thus, the great earth, six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in thickness, neither cracks nor disperses.
Brahmā! What do you think?
Was this created by you? Was it emanated by you?
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! When the ten billion suns and moons of this trichiliocosm revolve, Brahmā!
What do you think?”
"Is this what you have emanated?
Brahmā replied, "No,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said,
"Brahmā! There are times when the Sun and Moon Devas are not in their palaces, and the palaces are empty."
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something you have created, something you have emanated, or something you have empowered?"
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! Thus, regarding the seasons of spring, autumn, winter, and summer—what do you think?
Are these created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?”
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! It is thus:

water, mirrors, clarified butter, oil, mani-jewels, crystal, and other pure vessels manifest various forms—namely, the great earth, mountains, rivers, forests, gardens, palaces, houses, villages, towns, camels, donkeys, elephants, horses, deer, wild animals, birds, beasts, the sun, the moon, the constellations, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, tathāgatas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, humans, non-humans, and various other such forms.”
Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! It is thus:

the sounds produced by mountain cliffs and deep valleys, various drums large and small, songs, dances, and other performances, as well as the cries of deer, antelopes, birds, beasts, humans, and non-humans.”
Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! Just as all sentient beings, within their dreams, see various forms, hear various sounds, smell various fragrances, taste various flavors, feel various tactile sensations, cognize various phenomena, and engage in various play; they experience various weeping, moaning, fear, suffering, pleasure, and so forth.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Was this created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! Just as among people of the four castes there are those who are handsome or ugly, poor or extremely wealthy, possessing little or much merit, observing virtuous precepts or evil precepts, and possessing wholesome or unwholesome wisdom.”
Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?
Brahmā replied,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! All the fears, agonies, and afflictions of all sentient beings—namely, those arising from water, fire, swords, wind, precipices, poisons, wild beasts, enemies, and the fear of humans and non-humans, as well as various forms of injury—they are constantly in fear of others.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! Regarding all the various diseases of sentient beings—namely, those caused by wind, cold, heat, and miscellaneous ailments; those arising from the seasonal shifts and the disharmony of the four great elements; those inflicted by others; or those resulting from past karma—such as diseases of the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body; or furthermore, the various sufferings of mental anguish and feverish afflictions experienced by sentient beings.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā said: “No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! Whatever difficulties sentient beings face—such as wildernesses, treacherous bandits, or calamities from floods; or, furthermore, the intermediate kalpas of warfare, pestilence, and famine—O Brahmā!”
"What do you think?
Was this created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?
The Brahmā replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, "Brahmā!
The suffering of separation from those one loves that sentient beings experience—namely, the suffering of being separated from parents, brothers, sisters, kinsmen, and virtuous friends.
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! Regarding the various evil deeds committed by sentient beings—namely, the trade of living beings, wine and yeast, lac, and oil-pressing equipment; or traveling through the great oceans, wildernesses, and treacherous regions in all directions; or the incantations of the rishis and other various methods for resolving legal disputes.
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! Sentient beings perform various paths of karma; by means of these karmic causes, they undergo retribution as hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or devas.”

Whatever actions sentient beings perform through body, speech, and mind—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—and all the ten unwholesome paths of action in the world, which lack any compassion for other beings and result in causing them suffering and harm, are the causes and conditions for falling into the evil realms. These are: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! All the various kinds of suffering experienced by sentient beings—namely, having one’s head cut off, having one’s hands and feet severed, having one’s ears and nose sliced off, having one’s limbs and joints dismembered, being doused with boiling oil, being roasted or boiled over fire, being hacked, pierced, or beaten with swords, spears, lances, and whips, being imprisoned in jails, and engaging in quarrels and legal disputes.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! As for the sexual misconduct committed by sentient beings—whether it be with one’s mother, daughter, or sister, or with those who purely uphold the precepts—as well as other evil karmas.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! All the various forms of killing among sentient beings—such as using loathsome insects or reanimated corpses, incantations and medicinal prescriptions, possession by malevolent spirits, and other such diverse karmic expedients that sever life—are the causes and conditions for taking life.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā replied,
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! All that exists in the world—birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; all things that are impermanent, subject to exhaustion, and subject to change—discriminate against none of the four castes, and they cause the ruin and dispersal of all cherished and inexhaustible varieties of things.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
The Brahmā said,
“No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! All sentient beings are bound by the fetters and afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as by various other forms of suffering and distress. By these causes and conditions, because they cause sentient beings to be firmly attached to anger and confusion of mind, they perform immeasurable and diverse karmic actions.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā replied,
“No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! In all three evil destinies—the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts—sentient beings there undergo various forms of suffering and affliction for diverse reasons.”
Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! All that exists—whether produced from seeds or produced without seeds, such as trees and medicinal herbs;

whether growing in water or on land, such as flowers, fruits, and fragrant trees—possesses various superior flavors: sweet, bitter, salty, pungent, sour, and astringent. These act to benefit or harm according to what sentient beings find pleasing or displeasing.”
"Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?"
Brahmā said, “No,
World-Honored One!
The Buddha said:

“Brahmā! In the transmigration through the five realms, amidst the formation and destruction of birth and death, all sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and bound by the fetters of craving; they rush and wander about, their beginning and end difficult to know, and the continuity of their future transmigration through birth and death remains unbroken.

Whether humans or devas, whether Māras or Brahmās, śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas—these beings of the world are like tangled threads, constantly rushing and circulating, coming and going from one place to another; yet these sentient beings, amidst this cycle of transmigration, do not know how to seek liberation from it.
Brahmā! What do you think?
Is this something created by you, emanated by you, or empowered by you?
Brahmā said, "No, Blessed One. The Buddha said:
“Brahmā! For what reason do you entertain this thought, saying:
‘These sentient beings were created by me, transformed by me, and empowered by me’?”
"Are all worlds created by me, emanated by me, and empowered by me?
The Brahmā replied:
“World-Honored One!

Because I lacked wisdom and held wrong views, because I had not severed the mind of inversion, and because I did not listen to or accept the True Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata, I formerly held such evil views and made such evil declarations:
‘These sentient beings were created by me; they were emanated by me.’”
"All worlds are created by me; all worlds are emanated by me.
World-Honored One, I now ask the Buddha again about this matter: by whom were all these worlds created, and by whom were they emanated?
“By whom were all sentient beings created? By whom were they transformed? By whom were they empowered? By whose power were they brought into existence?
The Buddha said, “Brahmā!
All worlds are created by karma and transformed by karma;
all sentient beings are created by karma, transformed by karma, and born through the power of karma.
Why is this? Brahmā! Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations;

conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is clinging; conditioned by clinging is existence; conditioned by existence is birth; and conditioned by birth come old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. Thus there arises this entire mass of great suffering.

Brahmā! From the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, there is no agent, no instigator, and no establisher; there are only karma, dharmas, and the conjunction of causes and conditions, whereby sentient beings exist.
If one can be free from this karma, these phenomena, and their conjunction, you should know that such a person is able to remain far removed from the cycle of birth and death.
Brahmā! In this way, when worldly karma is exhausted, afflictions are exhausted, suffering is exhausted, and suffering comes to rest.
Such renunciation is called attaining the tranquil nirvāṇa.
"Brahmā! Who, therein, attains nirvāṇa?"

Whether it be karma that is the exhaustion of karma, afflictions that are the departure from afflictions, or suffering that is the cessation of suffering—such phenomena exist by virtue of the spiritual power of all Buddhas and through the empowerment bestowed by all Buddhas.
Why is this? Brahmā!
If it were not for the appearance in the world of the Buddhas who proclaim and explain them, one would not hear of such dharmas as these.

Brahmā! When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world, they are able to clearly expound such profound and difficult-to-realize dharma-gates of illumination as this samādhi of tranquility.
If sentient beings hear of the phenomenon of birth, they attain liberation from birth;

if they hear of the phenomena of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, they attain liberation from those phenomena of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction.
"Brahmā! For this reason, the Buddhas manifest this empowerment. Brahmā!"

The Buddhas provide this instruction and clear exposition, namely: all conditioned phenomena are like light and shadows—impermanent, shifting, unstable, non-final, subject to exhaustion, and subject to transformation.
Even if, after the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, the True Dharma should disappear, it is likewise so: they manifest their empowerment, showing that all conditioned phenomena are like light and shadows.

If all conditioned phenomena were like reflections and shadows in a mere instant when the Buddha does not appear, then one should not say that all conditioned phenomena are like reflections and shadows, like dreams, or like echoes.

“Brahmā! Because the Buddhas know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are like light and shadow, like a dream, like an echo, impermanent, shifting, subject to exhaustion, and subject to transformation, they declare that all conditioned phenomena are like light and shadow, like a dream, and like an echo.”

When the wise person has contemplated their characteristics, by means of those characteristics and by means of the principle of the causal conditions of the object of focus, they come to know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent, shifting, subject to exhaustion, subject to transformation, prone to destruction and dispersal, and subject to the passage of time.
In the space of a single kṣaṇa, and even throughout days, nights, half-months, months, years, hundreds of years, eons, and even hundreds of eons, everything is utterly destroyed.
There is a great mass of fire that, having burned, is extinguished;
there is a great mass of water that, having flowed, ceases;
there is a great, violent wind that, having blown, subsides.
The great earth of the world exists and then returns to non-existence;
there are great mountains—namely, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Mount Sumeru, and the various Black Mountains—which exist and then return to non-existence;
the sun, moon, constellations, and their retinues exist and then return to non-existence, becoming dim and unilluminating, and finally falling away.
The celestial palaces of the devas arise and then pass away;
all royal capitals, cities, towns, villages, groves, gardens, ponds, and all delightful things arise and then pass away;
and the various gods and humans arise and then pass away, and having passed away, they are born again.

"When those who possess wisdom see these signs, they give rise to a mind of weary detachment. Because these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, subject to separation, destruction, transformation, and exhaustion, they renounce their homes and go forth into homelessness with a mind of impartial faith, realizing that all conditioned phenomena are like shadows and light, like dreams, and like echoes."

Furthermore, having seen the reflections of the sun, moon, stars, and other celestial bodies in water, one attains bodhi by means of those signs, through the causal conditions of those objects of perception.

There are wise persons who, having received the Buddha’s instructions and the teachings of virtuous friends, or through their own reflection, come to know that all conditioned phenomena are like shadows and lights, like dreams, and like echoes; thus they give rise to faith and leave the household life to go forth.
Some attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat;
those of the Mahāyāna path either attained the first patience (kṣānti), or the second and third patiences, and were able to reach unsurpassed bodhi.
Even after the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas, the Dharma shall likewise circulate and spread throughout the world in this manner.

If sentient beings hear this Dharma, they shall attain deliverance through the three vehicles—namely, the vehicle of the śrāvakas, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, and the unsurpassed Great Vehicle of all-knowledge.
“Brahmā! You should know that this sequence of dharmas is also empowered by all the Buddhas.

Therefore, when a wise person perceives these signs, their mind gives rise to weary detachment; they are able to know that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are impermanent and suffering, shifting and unstable, subject to exhaustion and transformation, just like a reflection of light, a dream, or an echo.”
“Brahmā! These, too, are the domain of all Buddhas and are empowered by all Buddhas.
There are sentient beings who, having already practiced and accomplished the causes, upon hearing the sound of such true Dharma, conceive thoughts of reverence and faith toward the Tathāgata.”
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and subject to destruction, like a reflection of light, like a dream, and like an echo.

There are sentient beings who have previously practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in the presence of various Buddhas, or those living at home who have received the prohibitive precepts; by these causes and conditions, they understand and realize that all such conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to destruction, like a reflection of light, like a dream, and like an echo.
Having known this, they give rise to faith, renounce their homes, and go forth into homelessness.
Although the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have not yet appeared in the world, by virtue of such empowerments from the Buddhas and the roots of goodness planted by the Buddhas, one attains bodhi.
“Brahmā! You should know this: all of these are the realm of the Buddhas and are empowered by the Buddhas. Brahmā!”
This trichiliocosm is neither the realm of Brahmā nor the realm of the six heterodox teachers; it is solely the realm of us Buddhas.

“Brahmā! In the past, throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I cultivated the bodhisattva practices; in the presence of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Tathāgatas, I planted immeasurable asaṃkhyeya roots of goodness, purely observed the prohibitive precepts, diligently practiced the holy life, and performed immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of difficult and painful austerities to encompass this buddha-field, cultivating and purifying it.”

According to the roots of goodness cultivated by sentient beings, purifying them according to their capacity, and delivering them according to the appropriate time and vessel, I have throughout the long night gathered these sentient beings through the four means of attraction—namely, giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.

By the power of my vow, they shall be born in this buddha-field; upon hearing me preach the Dharma, they will immediately be able to believe and understand it, and will no longer place their faith in Brahmā, Śakra, the World-Protectors, or the various celestial kings.
Brahmā! You should know this:
this is a buddha-field; it is not the realm of Brahmā, Śakra, or the World-Protectors, nor is it the realm of the six heretical teachers.
At that time, Mahābrahmā, the lord of the Sahā world, together with a multitude of hundreds of thousands of Brahmās, manifested an expression of sorrow and spoke these words:
"The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have attained the rare, supreme, and wondrous Dharma."

Thus, Mahābrahmā, the Lord of this trichiliocosm, conceived a sense of rare wonder toward the Tathāgata: "How rare it is for the Buddhas! They possess immeasurable, inconceivable, and inexhaustible realms."
The Great Brahmā King immediately took refuge as a disciple of the Buddha and requested instructions from the World-Honored One, saying:
"The Bhagavān is my great teacher; the Sugata is my great teacher."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will instruct me: how should I abide?
How should I practice?
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"This trichiliocosm is my buddha-field; I now entrust it to you.

You should comply with me and ensure that the true path and the good eye are not allowed to be severed; do not allow the unsurpassed Buddha-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Sangha-eye to be severed; do not become one who causes the Dharma to perish at the end."
"Brahmā!

There shall be the eldest son, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya in his state of youthful innocence, born from the mouth of the Buddha and born through transformation by the Dharma, who out of great compassion and pity desires to benefit all sentient beings, desires to bring them happiness, and desires to establish them in peace and security."
He, too, is a successor who maintains the Dharma in this trichiliocosm, just as I abide here; there is no difference between us.

Since you are currently following my teachings, you should likewise follow him, so that this true path—the mother of the Dharma, the Buddha-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Sangha-eye—may never be severed.
Why is this? Brahmā!

As long as this mother of the Dharma is not severed, according to the appropriate seasons, the Buddha-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Saṅgha-eye shall not be interrupted; the eyes of Śakra, Brahmā, and the devas, the human eye, the eye of liberation, and even the eye of nirvāṇa shall not be interrupted.
Brahmā! For this reason, I now entrust to you this buddha-field, this trichiliocosm. Brahmā!
"I have already given my instructions; you should comply with them and do not become one who causes the Dharma to perish at the end.

At that time, all the Brahmās and Mahābrahmās throughout the trichiliocosm—each of whom had previously attained right faith in the Noble Dharma—the Great Brahmā King, Lord of the trichiliocosm, immediately attained profound right faith within the Noble Dharma.

Chapter Two: The Merchant Leader. *The Sutra of Great Compassion*, Chapter Two: The Merchant Leader. At that time, there was a son of Māra named Śreṣṭhin (Merchant Leader), who had attained profound faith and respect for the Buddha. Upon hearing that the Buddha was entering parinirvāṇa, his heart was filled with grief and distress; trembling with fear, his hair stood on end, and he hurried to the place where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I pray only that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for sentient beings, for the peace and happiness of sentient beings, to rescue and protect the world, and out of compassion and benefit for all devas and humans, will remain in the world for a kalpa and not enter parinirvāṇa."
Out of compassion for all devas and humans, I likewise entreat you thus: World-Honored One,
do not allow sentient beings to fall into blindness so soon, leaving them without one who speaks the Dharma, without a guide, without a savior, without a refuge, and without a destination.
At that time, having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed him, saying:
"Merchant Leader!
Your father Pāpīyas previously invited me to enter parinirvāṇa, speaking as follows:..."
"Bhagavān, enter parinirvāṇa! Sugata!"
"Entering parinirvāṇa!
Blessed One, now is precisely the time to enter nirvāṇa."
"O Caravan Leader!
Your father Pāpīyas entreated me in this manner, and I, in accordance with his wish, consented to enter parinirvāṇa.
O Caravan Leader!"
"For these reasons, the time has now arrived for me; therefore, in accordance with my promise, I shall enter nirvana.
The caravan leader spoke again:
"World-Honored One!"
This Māra Pāpīyān is not my father, nor is he my good friend.
He constantly seeks to kill and harm me; he is my enemy and a great evil associate.
He always desires that I may not obtain happiness, harmony, or peace, but only brings about destruction and does not wish for my benefit.
"Bhagavān!

This Māra is utterly intent on doing me evil; he slanders gods and humans and acts as a great adversary, constantly seeking to extinguish such a torch of wisdom, a light of wisdom, and a great lamp of clear intelligence."
"Bhagavān!
If there were a person of truthful speech who were to say:
'Among all gods and humans, there is one extremely poisonous and evil person who has appeared in the world.'"
"You should know that this is none other than Māra Pāpīyān.
World-Honored One!
If there were a person speaking words of truth who were to say this:"
"If there is one who generates the aspiration for enlightenment not for the sake of benefiting themselves, nor for the sake of others, nor for the sake of many sentient beings,
you should know that this person is none other than Māra Pāpīyān."
"Bhagavān!
Suppose there were another person who speaks words of truth and says:

'There is someone who does not act out of compassion for the benefit of gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, asuras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and the entire world; nor does he wish for their harmony and peace, but rather resolves his mind with the desire to cause them to fall away and suffer affliction.'"
"You should know that this is none other than Māra Pāpīyan.
"World-Honored One!

I have personally heard such a teaching from the Buddha: there are two kinds of people—the first is those who act in accordance with the Dharma, and the second is those who act contrary to the Dharma."
You should know that the Blessed One’s granting of permission for Pāpīyān to enter nirvāṇa is contrary to the Dharma.

We only pray that the Blessed One will not harbor firm attachment to this permission; rather, out of compassion and for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, including gods and humans, may you relinquish this permission and remain in the world for a kalpa.
"If the Buddha were to remain for a long time, all devas and humans would benefit and find peace and happiness; therefore, World-Honored One, do not enter parinirvāṇa too soon.
The Buddha told the merchant leader:
"Excellent, excellent!"
If one brings benefit to sentient beings, it should indeed be thus.
O Caravan Leader!

If a person provides for a consecrated Kṣatriya great king, or provides for a prince or a minister, or protects the kingdom, cities, towns, and villages, that person shall receive great honor and rank from that Kṣatriya king and enjoy his fortune and emoluments.
That Kṣatriya king will always bestow favor, fortune, and emoluments upon this person, as well as upon their descendants, friends, and kinsmen, and will protect and shelter them.
O Merchant Leader!

If you now give rise to pure faith in the mind toward the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, then because of that pure faith, the Tathāgata shall console you and grant you the reward of merit.
I now console you because you have conceived pure faith in the Buddha and planted roots of goodness.
Know this, caravan leader:
by means of these roots of goodness born of pure faith, after my parinirvāṇa, in a future age, you shall become a pratyekabuddha named Compassionate Caravan Leader.
"After my parinirvāṇa and the extinction of the True Dharma, this Māra Pāpīyān will experience great joy;
because of that joy, he shall fall from his demonic palace and be cast into the Avīci Great Hell, where he will undergo immeasurable varieties of suffering and affliction."
Why is this? Because Māra Pāpīyān experiences great joy when this lamp of supreme wisdom and light of wisdom are eclipsed and extinguished.
O Caravan Leader!
If there were a person of truthful speech who were to say this:
"There is someone who has generated the resolve for the sake of harming themselves, for their own ruin, and to do evil unto themselves."
"You should know that this is none other than Māra Pāpīyān. Why is this so,
Merchant Leader?"
After my parinirvāṇa, as long as this True Dharma remains in the world, Māra Pāpīyān shall remain in his palace according to the passage of time;

but once my Dharma has been extinguished, Māra will experience extreme joy, exultation, and celebration, feeling that his every desire has been fulfilled—only to fall from his palace in an instant and descend into the Avīci Hell.
“O Caravan Leader!

It is as if there were a person who climbed a great tree that was fully endowed with flowers and fruit; having taken the flowers and fruit to his heart’s content and enjoyed them, he then broke off the very branch upon which he had been sitting.”
"O caravan leader!
What do you think?
At that time, would that person, standing on those broken branches, be able to remain upon the tree?"
"Furthermore, having experienced pleasure under that tree, if one were to go back and break its branches,
could he be called wise? The merchant leader replied, "No, Blessed One!"
"No, Sugata! The Buddha said,
"Caravan Leader!"

Māra is likewise; he constantly desires that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha enter parinirvāṇa, and he always delights in concealing and extinguishing the True Dharma and Vinaya taught by the Tathāgata.
"O Caravan Leader!
As long as the True Dharma remains in the world, Māra Pāpīyān shall remain in his palace during that time;
but when my Dharma is extinguished, Māra Pāpīyān will give rise to great exultation, joy, and satisfaction, and for that reason he shall fall from his palace and descend into the Avīci Hell."
"O Caravan Leader!
Just as that person exerts himself in this task for the sake of harming himself upon that tree;
so too does Māra exert himself in generating the thought of enlightenment for the sake of harming himself and for the sake of harming others."
"O Caravan Leader!
At a later time, Māra will fall into the Avīci Hell and undergo great agony, like the pain of having one's life taken.
Once he has been touched by that suffering, he shall remember: "

"I declare that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks reality, one whose words do not differ from the fact, and one who does not speak falsely; thus he has well said:
'Excellent is restraint of body, excellent is restraint of speech, and excellent is restraint of mind.'"
These wholesome actions of body, these wholesome actions of speech, and these wholesome actions of mind result in fruits that are delightful, desirable, lovely, and agreeable;
whereas these unwholesome actions of body, these unwholesome actions of speech, and these unwholesome actions of mind result in fruits that are undelightful, undesirable, unlovely, and disagreeable.

"In the past, I was associated with misconduct of body, associated with misconduct of speech, and associated with misconduct of mind. Due to the retribution of these karmic actions, I have now fallen into hell, experiencing such extreme pain, extreme intensity, extreme suffering, extreme affliction, and extreme unbearability—like the agony of facing death."
"At that time, Māra Pāpīyān shall remember what I have said and attain pure faith;
having attained pure faith, he will immediately pass away from that hell and be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
Why is this so? O Caravan Leader!
If one with an evil mind commits various transgressions against the Tathāgata, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will fall into the great hells.

Furthermore, if one makes offerings with a mind of loving-kindness to the Tathāgata without seeking faults, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will be reborn among the gods or humans in the happy realms.
By means of those roots of goodness, one shall encounter various Buddhas;
having encountered the Buddhas, one shall again plant roots of goodness.
"Having planted these roots of goodness, you shall successively attain untainted nirvāṇa.
Caravan Leader!
Since you have attained pure faith in the mind toward the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, by virtue of these roots of goodness, you shall encounter Maitreya when he appears in the world."
Having encountered Maitreya, they will be able to awaken those sentient beings who are asleep and negligent, speaking these words:

"All you sentient beings should be courageous and diligently perform wholesome deeds! It is extremely difficult for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha to appear in the world; he appears only once in a great while, like the udumbara flower which blooms but at rare intervals.
The Tathāgata is likewise; he appears but once in a great while to enter the nirvāṇa that has no abode."
At that time, there were those who said:

"A human body is difficult to obtain; the eight states of no-leisure are difficult to escape from. To encounter the era of a Buddha and to be born in a central land is likewise exceedingly difficult."
"Therefore, you all must be careful not to be negligent; you should practice diligently so that you will have no regrets later.
"O Merchant Leader!

You shall receive the teachings from Maitreya Buddha and gather the people of that supreme Dharma-king Maitreya’s realm. Constantly with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind free of malice, a mind free of enmity, a mind of compassion, a mind of joy, and a mind of universal protection, you shall guard, sustain, and nourish them. By these roots of goodness, you shall succeed to the position of Māra within the palace of Māra, possessing great wealth and nobility, and becoming a sovereign lord."
"O Caravan Leader!

If there are sentient beings who plant various roots of goodness before the Tathāgata, even if they only manage to give rise to a single thought of pure mind, those sentient beings, by virtue of these roots of goodness, shall draw near to the nectar of immortality—the foremost nectar, the final nectar."
“Caravan leader!

Having extensively received the retributions of gods and humans there through your roots of goodness, after eighty kalpas have passed, in your final body you will become a pratyekabuddha named Compassionate.”
Why is this? Caravan leader!
Because upon hearing the sound of my parinirvāṇa, you have conceived pure faith toward me and a heart of compassion toward all sentient beings.
For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, you entreated me to remain and not enter parinirvāṇa;

furthermore, within the Dharma of that Maitreya, you will compassionately regard sentient beings, awakening those who are asleep and negligent, causing them to maintain mindfulness and avoid negligence, and instructing them in wholesome dharmas.
By these causes and conditions, you shall receive the prediction of becoming a pratyekabuddha.
"O caravan leader!
I shall grant you such a virtuous reward that you should feel deep joy and satisfaction in your heart.
O caravan leader!"
"These are the roots of goodness resulting from your exhortation of the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata now repays those roots of goodness by providing you with the protection of the gift of Dharma.
At that time, the merchant leader again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

If the Buddha does not accept my request for him to enter parinirvāṇa, I vow that from this day forth until the Dharma remains, I shall remain free from the five desires and devote myself exclusively to the path of filial piety; I shall take no pleasure in amusements, wear no exotic garments, use no flower garlands, unguents, or powdered incense, and refrain from enjoying the superior rewards of the devas.

Why is this? Because such a World-Honored One—a treasure to all sentient beings—will tomorrow part from me to dwell in another place; we shall never meet again, he will no longer exist, and he will ultimately be invisible.
World-Honored One!
What joy do I have?
What amusement do I have?
What is there to find joy in?
What is there to satisfy the mind?
If such a supreme torch of wisdom, a lamp of wisdom, and the radiance of great knowledge were to vanish and be extinguished, what cause for exultation, satisfaction, or celebration would I have?

This great sun of wisdom, which possesses immeasurable hundreds of thousands of rays of light as its retinue to dispel the great darkness of ignorance and produce the illumination of great wisdom—now that it has thus set and vanished, how could I have any joy or satisfaction?
What is there to find joy in?
What is there to laugh at?

For I am separated from such jewels among sentient beings—those who measure all beings, those who are without deficiency, those endowed with clarity, those without fault, those without delusion, those who are unsurpassed, those who are supreme, those without peer, those without equal, those equal to the unequaled, those capable of saving all beings, those who are wondrous among beings, those who are worthy of offerings by beings, and those who share the same vehicle as beings.

He is the tamer of sentient beings, the compassionate one toward sentient beings, the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker at the proper time, the speaker according to the occasion, and the speaker of that which does not differ from what he says;

he is one who practices according to his words, one who dwells in great loving-kindness and compassion, one whose mind has no hindrance toward any sentient being, and one who possesses a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings;

he is free from conceptual proliferation, free from the notions of "self" and "mine," free from accumulation, free from a dwelling place, free from dependence, free from desolate wilderness, and free from defilement.
He is the savior, the guide, the deliverer, the preparer, the unbinder, and the nurturer;

he causes sentient beings to remember, awakens them, and instructs them; he is victorious in battle, the one who extracts arrows, the king of physicians who heals the mind, the giver of great and excellent medicine, the one who brings an end to suffering, and the teacher of the Dharma;

he is the caravan leader about to depart, the one who shows the shallow waters, the one who holds the rudder, the one who holds the torch, the maker of light, the maker of radiance, the illuminator, the giver of eyes, and the one who points the way.

He causes them to reach the land of peace and security; he causes them to be far removed from all wildernesses and defilements; he is free from craving; he is free from all messengers; he is free from all fetters; he is free from greed, hatred, and delusion; he is free from all afflictions; he is free from arrogance and anger.

Such a great man, a sublime man, a supreme man, a heroic man, a fierce man, a lotus-like man, a white lotus-like man, a nāga-like man, a nāga-teacher-like man, a lion-like man, a preeminent man, a formidable man, a valiant man, an elephant-like man, an unsurpassed man, and an unsurpassed tamer of men.

He is one who rides together with all beings; one endowed with all powers; one endowed with the ten powers; one who has attained the four fearlessnesses; one endowed with the eighteen unique qualities; one who has attained the power of great merit and wisdom; one who has fulfilled the immeasurable treasury of Dharma;
one free from envy; one who brings joy to all sentient beings; the unsurpassed supreme donor; the most excellent donor;

one whose mind is free from resentment; one who has attained great meditative concentration; one who has attained the spheres of all dhyānas, samādhis, and samāpattis; one of immeasurable wisdom; one of unobstructed wisdom; and one who has attained the sphere of incomparable wisdom.

He who has crushed the banner of Māra, who has crossed the mire, who has reached the further shore, who dwells on the further shore, who has arrived at the state of fearlessness, who has removed the terrors of all sentient beings, who comforts all sentient beings, and who is the steadfast refuge for the great multitudes—this very night, in the final watch, we shall be separated from him; we shall never see him again.
“World-Honored One!
Since we shall no longer hear the Tathāgata’s true lion’s roar amidst the great assemblies, how could I feel any joy or satisfaction?
World-Honored One!”

For example, suppose there is a person who has received wealth and honor from a consecrated Kṣatriya king; after that king passes away, he experiences great sorrow and suffering—recognizing the king’s nurturing kindness, recollecting the king’s nurturing kindness, and appreciating the king’s nurturing kindness—that being, for the sake of his king, single-mindedly maintains the way of filiality, weeping as he recalls him for one day, two days, up to seven days, or even for half a month or a full month.
World-Honored One!

I am likewise; from the time after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa until the end of the True Dharma remaining in the world, I shall, according to the seasons, renounce the five desires and devote myself exclusively to the way of filial piety. I shall take no pleasure in play or laughter, wear no unusual garments, nor use flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, or enjoy any of the fruits of celestial retribution.

Chapter 3: Śakra. In the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Three, "Śakra," at that time, Śakra Devānām-indra went to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, he prostrated himself, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will instruct me: how should I practice?"
“World-Honored One!
Once upon a time, the four great asura kings, having harnessed their chariots and donned their armor, led their retinues to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, desiring to engage in battle.”
At that time, the noble Maudgalyāyana was still dwelling in the world.
When the devas and asuras were thus arrayed for battle, the noble Maudgalyāyana went to the four asuras and subdued them in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, all the devas and asuras attained peace and security; they were no longer subject to the suffering of battle, nor did they harbor mutual hostility, slander, or contentious debate.
World-Honored One!

Now that this Mahāmaudgalyāyana has already entered parinirvāṇa, and the Tathāgata now likewise intends to enter parinirvāṇa, we shall repeatedly engage in conflict and act in mutual opposition in the future.
"I pray that you will grant me your instruction: when the four Asura kings go to war with me, what stratagem should I employ against them?
The Buddha addressed Śakra Devānām Indra, saying: "Kauśika!..."
Cease! Do not grieve, do not lament, do not worry, and do not brood.
For one who upholds the precepts, whatever they wish for will surely be accomplished; it is achieved only by one of pure morality, not by one of impure morality.

It is achieved by one who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), not by one who does not; by one who is free from desire, not by one who is not; by one who is free from hatred, not by one who is not; by one who is free from delusion, not by one who is not; and by one who possesses wisdom, not by one who lacks wisdom. Thus it is achieved.
Kauśika! From this day forward, I shall bestow my protective empowerment upon you. Kauśika!
Until my True Dharma has ceased to exist, should there be any devas, asuras, and others who engage in mutual combat, the devas shall prevail at those times by virtue of invoking my name.

At that time, when the four great asura kings heard the Buddha speak these words of empowerment, their hearts were filled with resentment and indignation; their hair stood on end in terror, and they came to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason has the Tathāgata bestowed such empowerment?"
The Buddha addressed the four great asuras, saying:
"Do not grieve, do not worry.

There will come a time when you shall attain great sovereignty, surpassing even those in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where there is no further fighting, no strife, no rivalry, and no mutual opposition."
Therefore, you all must be careful not to engage in combat, not to revile one another, not to dispute with one another, and do not harbor contrary intentions;
you should instead cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, so that you may obtain the fulfillment of all desires.
O virtuous ones!
Life does not endure for long; even those who are sovereign lords are likewise impermanent.
O virtuous ones!
All that exists in this world, though complete and joined together, must inevitably return to separation.
O virtuous ones!

You should observe that the Tathāgata has reached the ultimate limit of impermanence; toward all sentient beings, he harbors no resentment or enmity, no opposition, and no contention, but always acts for their harmony and reconciliation.
All sentient beings resolve their minds toward enlightenment with equanimity; how much more so should you, who possess meager roots of goodness and delight in mutual strife and contention?
O worthy ones!
If there are those who give rise to the intention to harm or injure others, such persons will themselves suffer harm for a long night.
O virtuous ones!
If a person delights in killing, that person will receive the retribution of a short life.
If one delights in strife and contention, such a person will always live in fear of the retribution of death, lack a great retinue, and possess no great power.
O virtuous ones!
The two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—never perish.

Therefore, from this day forward, each of you should abide in a mind of loving-kindness—abiding in loving-kindness of bodily action, loving-kindness of verbal action, and loving-kindness of mental action—and do not fight, do not compete, and do not disparage one another.
"By these causes and conditions, you shall obtain benefit and peace for a long night, and later you will have no regrets.
Having spoken these words, the four asura kings addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!
We rely upon the teaching of the Tathāgata in this way, practicing and dwelling in this way."
“World-Honored One!
From this day forward, we shall all renounce our weapons of war and each cultivate a mind of loving-kindness.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, having heard of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, was pierced by the arrow of grief; overcome with extreme sorrow and distress, he wept with streaming tears and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
From this day forth until the Dharma remains, I shall not receive the five desires, I shall not enter the inner palace, and I shall not wear unusual garments.
O Great Virtuous Bhagavat!”

For example, when the head of a household passes away, those who were his acquaintances and received his kindness and support feel mental anguish; recollecting his past favors and mindful of his nurturing care, they weep with flowing tears and single-mindedly uphold the way of filial piety.
World-Honored One!

I am likewise; for as long as the Dharma remains, I shall weep and shed tears according to the seasons, single-mindedly upholding the way of filiality, refraining from the five desires, not entering the inner palace, and not wearing unusual garments.
"Why is this? The Unsurpassed Guide shall depart tomorrow; we shall no longer be able to see him, nor shall we ever meet again.
Having spoken these words, Śakra Devānām Indra immediately bowed his face to the ground and remained there weeping.
The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Scroll One.
The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Scroll Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Four: Rāhula. At that time, the Venerable Rāhula had this thought:
"What joy, what satisfaction, or what cause for celebration could I possibly have to endure seeing the World-Honored One enter parinirvāṇa with my own eyes?"
Having formed this thought, to the northeast, ten Buddha-fields from here, there is a world named Mālīci, where the Buddha is named Duryodhana Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula vanished from the birthplace of the Mallas in the city of Kuśinagara and proceeded toward the northeast, to where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Duṣprasaha was residing.
Having arrived, he prostrated himself in salutation and withdrew to stand to one side, sorrowful and unhappy.
At that time, the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha addressed Rāhula, saying: "Rāhula!
"Do not grieve or lament,
Rāhula! All things that are beloved and agreeable, being conditioned and composite, must inevitably be separated."
Rāhula! It is the nature of all things that when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have completed their Buddha-work, they all enter parinirvāṇa. Rāhula!
"You should return there.

Now the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, in the space between the twin śāla trees at the birthplace of the Malla, lies on his right side like a lion king; this very day, during the last watch of the night, he will enter parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder."
"Rāhula! You must certainly go; after the Buddha-Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, you will surely feel grief and regret.
When he had spoken these words, Rāhula addressed the Buddha Duṣprasaha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I cannot bear to hear the sound of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni entering nirvāṇa; how much less could I bear to see that Buddha, the World-Honored One, enter parinirvāṇa?”
"Therefore, I cannot bear to go there.

At that time, having answered the Buddha Difficult to Conquer (Duṣprasaha), Rāhula vanished from that place and traveled upward, passing through ninety-nine worlds until he reached the hundredth world. There, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Caravan Leader (Sārthavāha) currently dwells in the world.
At that time, Rāhula arrived, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and stood to one side, weeping piteously with streaming tears and wailing in sorrow.
Once he was standing to one side, the Buddha Bhagavat, the Lord of Merchants, said to Rāhula: "Stop."
Rāhula! Do not grieve. Rāhula!

Regarding all phenomena: that what is born is not born, what is aging does not age, what is ill is not ill, what is dying does not die, and what is exhausted is not exhausted—such a thing is impossible.
Rāhula! The Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the past have entered parinirvāṇa through the cessation and detachment [of all things];
the Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas of the future will enter parinirvāṇa through the cessation and detachment [of all things].
The present Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas have entered parinirvāṇa through the stillness of detachment. Rāhula!
Even if the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for one kalpa or a hundred kalpas, he would inevitably enter parinirvāṇa in this very manner.
Rāhula! For all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, there is no other dharma besides this ultimate, quiescent nirvāṇa. Rāhula!

That which is ultimate quiescence is the ultimate concentration, the ultimate coolness, the ultimate exhaustion, the ultimate bliss, and the ultimate security—namely, the realm of nirvāṇa, which is without abode.

Rāhula! Birth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; separation from what is loved is suffering; encountering what is hated is suffering; not obtaining what one seeks is suffering; and the burden of the five aggregates is suffering—all such things are indeed suffering.
Rāhula! Only nirvāṇa is bliss. "Rāhula! [he said].
"You, too, shall before long enter parinirvāṇa. Rāhula!

The place where you and Śākyamuni Buddha enter nirvāṇa is free from birth, old age, sickness, and death; it is free from separation from the beloved, free from meeting with the hated, and free from anything disagreeable."
Rāhula! Do not grieve with longing, do not sorrow, and do not lament. Rāhula!
You should reflect:
who is it that is born?
Who is it that ages?
Who is it that dies?
Who is it that transmigrates?
And who is it that is born again?
Rāhula! All this arises from false, inverted grasping and attachment, due to not having heard the noble Dharma.

Because these ordinary worldlings have not seen the noble ones, have not had faith in the noble Dharma, have not studied the noble Dharma, have not understood the noble Dharma, have not known the noble Dharma, and have not dwelt in the noble Dharma, their minds are characterized by inverted perceptions and inverted views.
Due to inversion, there is birth; due to birth, there is aging; due to aging, there is death.
Having died, one is born again, rushing and wandering through the cycle of existence, withered and ruined, filled with craving and sorrow, beating one's breast and wailing.
Rāhula! All noble ones bring all conditioned activities to rest solely through this Dharma-vinaya; beyond this, there is nothing further to be done. Rāhula!
Thus, the Guide has completed what was to be done, and his śrāvaka disciples have completed what was to be done; there is nothing further to be done beyond this. Rāhula!
"Do not grieve, do not lament, and do not despair. Rāhula!

That Śākyamuni Buddha, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, is the most honored among the Śākyas; you should go to him now for a final prostration, offering, and veneration, lest you later fall into sorrow and regret after his parinirvāṇa."
“Rāhula! That Śākyamuni Buddha is now in the Śāla grove at the birthplace of the Mallas, lying on his right side like a lion king. He wishes to see you, Rāhula; you must certainly go.”
Having spoken these words, the Venerable Rāhula addressed the Buddha, the Lord of Merchants, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I cannot bear to hear the report that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni is entering parinirvāṇa; how much less could I bear to witness that Buddha, the World-Honored One, actually entering parinirvāṇa?”
Having spoken these words, his body and mind were overwhelmed with distress, and he could not sustain himself; he spoke again:
"That Blessed One Śākyamuni—the Honored One among the Śākyas, the Unsurpassed Dharma King, the Jewel among sentient beings—how can I now bear to witness that Buddha entering parinirvāṇa?"

The one who has compassion for all the world, whose physical form is peerless among all the world, who acts as a lamp for all the world, who acts as eyes for all the world, who acts as a torch of wisdom for all the world, and who illuminates all the world—tomorrow he will depart and pass away, and there shall be nothing left of him.
When he had spoken these words, the Tathāgata Śreṣṭhin said to Rāhula: "Stop, Rāhula!"
Do not grieve or lament,
Rāhula! Have you not heard that the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, has taught such a Dharma as this?
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are suffering; all phenomena are non-self; cessation is nirvana. Rāhula!
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; They are of the nature of arising and ceasing.
Having arisen, they pass away; Their cessation is bliss."
Rāhula replied, “So it is,
World-Honored One! The Buddha said to Rāhula:
“Did that Blessed One not previously say this:
‘All things that are loved and agreeable must inevitably return to destruction; before long they shall be separated;
even if they endure for a long time, there will surely come a time of parting.’”
Rāhula replied: “So it is, Blessed One!”
"So it is, Sugata! The Buddha said, "Rāhula!"
All conditioned phenomena—phenomena that arise, exist, are cognized, and originate through conceptual differentiation—are born from causes and conditions; it is impossible for them not to cease.
At that time, Rāhula, having called to mind his father, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, spoke with tears flowing:
"Tomorrow I shall no longer see the Buddha, surrounded by the assembly of bhikṣus as he preaches the Dharma—like Sumeru, the king of mountains, adorned with all its majesties amidst the great ocean;
like the full moon emitting radiance surrounded by the host of stars; like the sun with its thousand rays shining through the sky."

Like the deep great ocean, a place where immeasurable treasures are stored and accumulated; like a wheel-turning monarch, surrounded by an immeasurable retinue; like the king of snow mountains, where the flowers of the roots of power and awakening are in full bloom;
like Mount Cakravāḍa, which cannot be moved by any fierce winds—so too the World-Honored One cannot be shaken by the winds of the various disputations of all non-Buddhists;
and just as a lotus flower dwelling in a pond cannot be defiled by worldly conditions.
He is like Mahābrahmā surrounded by his Brahma retinue;
like Śakra possessing a thousand eyes;
like a lion king seated upon a lion throne, free from all fear, having abandoned every dread, and capable of uttering the lion’s roar—"Tomorrow I shall not see him again."
When Rāhula had spoken these words, he remained silent, weeping with grief, lost in contemplation.
At that time, the Tathāgata Śreṣṭhin addressed Rāhula, saying:
"You should now go quickly to where that Buddha is; that Tathāgata desires to see you."
Rāhula! You should depart quickly;
do not ask further questions so as to cause delay, and take care not to trouble that Blessed One, the World-Honored One. Rāhula!
"You must certainly go.
Why is that? Rāhula!"
"It is the natural law of all Buddhas that when a Buddha, out of compassion, desires to see you, he does not enter parinirvāṇa.

At that time, Rāhula prostrated with his head at the feet of that Lord of Merchants, the Buddha. Then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, and as quickly as the time it takes to extend or bend an arm, Rāhula vanished from that place and arrived at the presence of the Tathāgata between the twin śāla trees in the birthplace of the Mallas at Kuśinagara; it was just so.

Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and then stood to one side, weeping in sorrowful grief with palms joined and tears streaming down.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Rāhula, saying: “Rāhula!
Do not grieve, lament, weep, or let your mind be consumed by distress.
Rāhula! You have fulfilled your filial duties toward your father, and I too have fulfilled my paternal duties toward you.
Rāhula! Do not give rise to attachment, nor feel sorrow, grief, or regret. Rāhula!
Together with you all, for the sake of enabling all sentient beings to attain fearlessness, I have aroused diligent vigor;
and so that we may not act as enemies or cause harm and affliction, I have aroused great vigor.
Rāhula! Now that I have entered parinirvāṇa, I shall no longer act as a father to anyone else. Rāhula!
"You, too, shall enter parinirvāṇa; you shall no longer be the son of another. Rāhula!
Between me and you, both of us shall neither cause disturbance nor harbor enmity."
At that time, Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One! Bhagavān!”
Do not enter parinirvāṇa,
Sugata! Do not enter parinirvāṇa!

I only pray that the World-Honored One will remain in the world for one kalpa, for the sake of the peace, security, and happiness of the great multitude; out of compassion for the world; and for the benefit, peace, and happiness of all devas and humans.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha addressed Rāhula, saying: “Rāhula!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha fully knows all phenomena; for this reason, he is named ‘Buddha’ within the world.”

Rāhula! Yet that Buddha-dharma is neither consumed nor exhausted; it is neither born nor extinguished; it neither comes nor goes; it is neither formed nor destroyed; it neither sits nor lies down; it is neither joined nor dispersed.
Why is this? Rāhula! Such is the abiding of phenomena:

they are ultimately unarisen, ultimately unceasing, ultimately empty, and ultimately devoid of intrinsic nature; they are quiescent nirvāṇa, not included within the categories of things, without a dwelling place, ineffable, and beyond the path of language—this is the Dharma of all Buddhas.
That is to say: because it is ultimately abiding; because it is ultimately extinguished;
because it is ultimately quiescent; because it is ultimately detached;
because it is ultimately free from desire; and because it is ultimately non-composite.
Because they are ultimately unproduced and ultimately exhausted. Rāhula!

I have taught this Dharma according to what is appropriate. Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear in the world, these dharmas remain; such is the nature of dharmas, because dharmas are thus, because dharmas are immutable, because dharmas are free from desire, and because dharmas lack intrinsic nature.

Rāhula! In this way, the Tathāgata does not bring the aggregate of morality into parinirvāṇa, nor does he bring the aggregates of concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation into parinirvāṇa.
Rāhula! Do not grieve with longing, do not be sorrowful, do not be distressed. Rāhula!
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, unstable, and devoid of anything to be hoped for; they are impermanent and subject to exhaustion and transformation.
Rāhula! One should even bring all conditioned phenomena to rest, becoming weary of them, relinquishing them, and not clinging to them, seeking only liberation.
“Rāhula! This is my teaching.

When the Buddha spoke this Chapter on Seeing the True Truths for Rāhula, sixty great bhikṣus, all of whom were venerable, had their outflows exhausted and attained liberation of mind; twenty-five bhikṣuṇīs also attained liberation of mind and had their outflows exhausted; immeasurable devas and humans became free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye; and sixty-eight thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. All were filled with joy and exultation, praising the inconceivability of the Buddha-dharma.
They all scattered *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers over the Buddha and each spoke these words:

“In a future age, we too shall likewise become teachers of gods and humans, appearing in the world to proclaim such a Dharma—the unsurpassed, signless Nirvāṇa of the world—and thus enter parinirvāṇa through the Great Nirvāṇa.”
After those bodhisattvas had spoken these words, they remained silent.

Chapter Five: Kāśyapa. At that time, Ānanda was by the Buddha’s couch, weeping and shedding tears; he fainted and fell to the ground like a great tree cut down on the edge of a cliff, and spoke thus: “Bhagavān!
Nirvāṇa is too soon! Sugata,
Nirvāṇa is too soon!
The jewel among sentient beings, the one of great compassion, has vanished too soon;
the great lamp of the world, the great torch of the world, the most excellent among gods and humans, has vanished too soon;
the white lotus among sentient beings within this world has vanished too soon.
The elephant among beings—one who is well-disciplined himself, who further disciplines others, and who brings those not yet disciplined to discipline—has vanished too soon;
the unsurpassed guide, who can show the world the path to peace and security, has vanished too soon.
The Eye of Wisdom of the World—whose great light shines everywhere, able to reveal the world—has vanished far too soon; the world is now blind and dark, without a guide.
The Father and Mother of sentient beings have vanished from the world far too soon; the world is left orphaned and solitary, with nothing upon which to rely.
“O Jewel among sentient beings!
Why shall I not see you again tomorrow, when only your name remains?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Cease, Ānanda! Do not grieve."
I have already told you that all things beloved and pleasing, being phenomena of conjunction, must inevitably undergo separation. Ānanda!

Regarding all conditioned phenomena—phenomena that arise, phenomena that exist, phenomena that are perceived, phenomena produced by causes and conditions, and phenomena subject to destruction—if they were not to perish, such a thing would be impossible.
If he were to remain, that too would be impossible.
Ānanda! Even if he were to remain for a long time, such is the nature of all phenomena: there must inevitably be separation.
"Therefore, Ānanda, do not grieve or lament.

At that time, Ānanda gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, his eyes never wavering for a moment; having reflected thus, he too collapsed to the ground, like a great tree cut down on the edge of a precipice.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
"Ānanda! Cease; do not grieve or lament. Do not cause me to remain in the world through your grief and lamentation."
"Ānanda!
I have told you before: all things that are loved and pleasing, being conditioned and compounded, must inevitably be separated from;
even if they endure for a long time, their meeting must eventually end. Such is the nature of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-dharma)."

Ānanda! You have served the Tathāgata with loving-kindness and filial piety through both body and speech; your mind of immeasurable peace and happiness is free from duality, without anger, without resentment, and without enmity.
At that time, Ānanda rose from the ground, wiped away his tears, and said:
“World-Honored One!
How could I not be sorrowful?”
How could I not be sorrowful?

Tomorrow I shall be separated from such a great jewel among sentient beings—one of such great compassion, who has emerged from all worlds, who pities all worlds, who is cherished by all worlds, who is the refuge for all worlds, who guides all worlds, who benefits all worlds, and who brings peace and happiness to all worlds.
At that time, after Ānanda had wailed loudly, he wiped away his tears and said:
"How extraordinary, how extraordinary!

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are like corpses that commit acts of deception and oppression; they have caused this great lamp, this great torch, this great radiance of the sun, with its immeasurable flames and its retinue of hundreds of thousands of billions of *nayuta* of flame-banners—this one who universally manifests throughout the world as the object of vision, knowledge, mindfulness, and wisdom—to vanish so very swiftly from among the great jewels of sentient beings."
The one of great wisdom, the one of great radiance, has now vanished from the world too soon; the world is left desolate.
The one who provides protection has vanished too soon.
The Tathāgata, endowed with supernormal powers and transformations, has now vanished from the world too soon.
World-Honored One!
How could I not be sorrowful?
How could I not be grief-stricken?
"Bhagavān!
I am now astonished that my heart does not shatter into a hundred pieces.
Bhagavān!"

I too am personally astonished that I have not met my end before the Buddha; it must be that the World-Honored One has bestowed his supernatural power upon me, and for this reason, I have not met my end.

Why is this? It is because I have personally received and been taught in the presence of the Buddha the eighty-four thousand treasuries of the Dharma, which I have upheld without forgetting; however, I have not yet widely disseminated them among the devas and humans throughout the ten directions.
“World-Honored One!
Because I am sustained by the supernatural power of the Tathāgata, for this reason I shall not pass away.
World-Honored One!”
"How could I not be distressed?
How could I not be sorrowful,
World-Honored One?"
When I arrive at the city of Kapilavastu, the birthplace of the World-Honored One, where the Śākyas have gathered, what words shall I speak?
Shall I say that the Buddha Śākyamuni of the Solar Clan, the Honored One among the Śākyas and the Unsurpassed Dharma King, has entered parinirvāṇa?
When I arrive at Rājagṛha, what words shall I speak to King Ajātaśatru, the son of Vaidehī?
Shall I say that the Great Teacher, the Sun of Buddhas, has set; that the Physician-King, who could extract the arrows of the karma of immediate retribution from the world, has departed?
"What kind of words should I speak when I arrive in the city of Śrāvastī?
May I say that the One of Great Compassion who takes pity on the world has vanished and departed?
When I reach the Jeta Grove, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada will ask me:"
"When will the Tathāgata come to reside in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park?
What words shall I use in reply?
When I arrive before the Licchavis in the city of Vaiśālī, what words shall I speak?"
Can it be said that the Great Honored Teacher who has compassion for the world has vanished?
When good sons and good daughters from all directions come to inquire about the meaning of the Dharma, what words will you speak in response?
"Can it be that this Great Wise One, the wise one of the world, the dispeller of all doubts, has passed away?

For I no longer see the community of bhikṣus from all directions who, desiring to see the Buddha, come to offer worship, pay homage, and inquire after the World-Honored One; nor do I see those who come for the sake of the *poṣadha*, or those who come to ask about the Dharma or its meaning, nor do I hear them speaking of the attainment of the states of superior men."
