After the Blessed One has passed into extinction, such practitioners of the holy life who possess supernatural powers and transformations will vanish from the world; how could I not be sorrowful?
How could I not be grieved?
Having spoken these words, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "Ānanda!
Stop; do not grieve."
"My Brahma-faring shall be widely disseminated and long endure in the world, benefiting devas and humans. Ānanda!

Four hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, Kāśyapa, together with you and all the disciples, shall successively inherit [the lineage], performing supernatural transformations and practicing the Brahma-faring to benefit devas and humans."
Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament.
My True Dharma shall spread widely and abide long in the world, benefiting devas and humans.

Ānanda! After my parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣu Kāśyapa and you shall together resolve your minds to increase all virtues and prevent the loss of the unsurpassed *samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma that I have accumulated over incalculable hundreds of millions of nayutas of kalpas.
Why is this? Ānanda!

This bhikṣu Kāśyapa has few desires and is content; he is diligent in seclusion, delights in non-forgetfulness of mindfulness, delights in the absence of frivolous proliferation, and has concentration and wisdom manifest before him.
Ānanda! The bhikṣu Kāśyapa is able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the great assembly; he tirelessly teaches the Dharma regarding the holy life to all, just like a father and mother.

Ānanda! The bhikṣu Kāśyapa has a vision that reaches far beyond the fourfold assembly; out of compassion for the world and desiring to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings—both gods and humans—he has given rise to such a mind.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
To how many multitudes of devas and humans does the bhikṣu Kāśyapa bring benefit, peace, and happiness by thus generating the resolve for enlightenment?"
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! When the bhikṣu Kāśyapa entered nirvāṇa, he made this vow:”

"I pray that after my parinirvāṇa, through the empowerment of my supernatural power, my body and robes shall remain unchanged and undecayed; likewise, my hair, eyebrows, complexion, and all my sense organs and limbs shall remain unchanged and undecayed until the time when Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world, so that this body of mine may behold that World-Honored One and participate in his first assembly."

In this way, at the second and third great assemblies, through the empowerment of my vow-power, I shall cause many hundreds of sentient beings, many thousands of sentient beings, many tens of millions of sentient beings, and many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of sentient beings to attain the fruits of the noble path.

If Maitreya Buddha sees that my body and robes remain unchanged and undecayed, and if the śrāvakas of his three assemblies likewise see my body, my faculties, my limbs and joints, and my *kāṣāya* robe as unchanged and undecayed;
thereafter, my body shall abide in mid-air, and I shall cremate it with the fire of my own body. Once the body has been cremated, neither ashes nor charcoal shall remain.
"Ānanda! This was Kāśyapa’s resolve to bring benefit, welfare, and happiness to sentient beings. Ānanda!"
"Ānanda! Because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa was sustained by such power of aspiration, he brought these sentient beings to maturity and then entered parinirvāṇa."
"After the bhikṣu Kāśyapa has entered parinirvāṇa, four stone mountains shall come toward him and cover his body, merging together into one.
Ānanda!"

This body of Kāśyapa remains within those four stone mountains, its physical form neither decaying nor perishing. Until Maitreya Buddha appears in the world, for that entire duration, the body of the bhikṣu Kāśyapa shall remain intact and undecayed, and his saṃghāṭī robe shall likewise remain intact and undecayed.
Why is this? Ānanda!
Those who uphold the pure precepts, cultivate the holy life, and possess wisdom are able to fulfill their aspirations.
This cannot be accomplished by one who lacks pure precepts, does not cultivate the holy life, and possesses desire rather than wisdom.
Ānanda! It is because the Bhikṣu Kāśyapa was previously empowered by the force of his vow that he has entered parinirvāṇa.

After he has entered parinirvāṇa, that body of Kāśyapa shall remain forever unchanging and undecayed; his hair, body hair, blood, flesh, sense organs, limbs, joints, and even his robes shall likewise remain unchanging and undecayed, and his body shall not emit any odor, lasting until the time of Maitreya.
“Ānanda! When that Maitreya Buddha appears in the world, he will go together with his first assembly of nine hundred and sixty million bhikṣus to the place where Kāśyapa is.”
Ānanda! This Maitreya Buddha will manifest in the body of Kāśyapa to those nine hundred and sixty million bhikṣus and address them thus: "O bhikṣus!"

This bhikṣu Kāśyapa is a great śrāvaka within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; he dwells in the superior dhūta practices, is of few desires and contented, is diligent in seclusion, delights in non-distraction, and delights in the absence of frivolous proliferation. With concentration and wisdom manifest before him, he is able to instruct, benefit, and gladden the great multitude, preaching the Dharma for all those in the holy life without weariness, like a father or mother.
"O bhikṣus!
This bhikṣu Kāśyapa is far-sighted regarding the fourfold assembly; he is ultimately free from doubt and accords with the great multitude.
O bhikṣus!"
"Observe, Ānanda, how Kāśyapa, out of compassion for the world and desiring to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all gods and humans, has given rise to such a mind.
"Ānanda! [he continued].
During the second assembly of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Maitreya, nine billion four hundred million śrāvakas will come together to his place;
during the third assembly, nine billion two hundred million śrāvakas will likewise come to the place of Kāśyapa.
Ānanda! That Maitreya Buddha will address those twelve billion bhikṣus, saying:

"This bhikṣu Kāśyapa was the greatest śrāvaka within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; he dwelt in the superior dhūta practices, having few desires and being content, even to the point of generating the resolve for the sake of benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all devas and humans."
"Ānanda! At that time, the Tathāgata Maitreya shall extend his golden right hand, stroke the crown of Kāśyapa’s head, and observe the bhikṣus, saying: 'Bhikṣus!'"

This bhikṣu Kāśyapa, after the parinirvāṇa of Śākyamuni Buddha, will extensively uphold the True Dharma; yet among this assembly, there is not a single person who, after my parinirvāṇa, will be able to extensively uphold my True Dharma as Kāśyapa does.

“Ānanda! At that third great assembly, this bhikṣu Kāśyapa, through the empowerment of his original vow, will abide in mid-air and manifest various supernatural powers and various transformations. Having done so, he will cremate his own body with the fire from his own person;
once the body has been cremated, neither ashes nor charcoal shall remain.”

At that time, after Maitreya Buddha has brought forth the realization of Kāśyapa, he will repeatedly preach the Dharma for the assembly of ninety-two billion bhikṣus; many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of millions of nayutas of devas and humans will attain the fruits of the noble paths.

“Ānanda! The bhikṣu Kāśyapa has resolved his mind for the sake of benefiting many sentient beings; you, too, have resolved your mind for the sake of benefiting, bringing peace, and happiness to many sentient beings.”
Thus it is, Ānanda!

Because the bhikṣu Kāśyapa and you have both resolved your minds [upon this], for four hundred years after my passing, you shall be able to uphold my True Dharma, manifest various supernatural transformations through your supernormal powers, and practice the holy life, each of you increasing the assembly of devas and humans.
6. Chapter on Upholding the True Dharma. *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, Chapter Six: Upholding the True Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Do not grieve or lament. My pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) shall be widely disseminated, and each person shall be able to increase the assembly of devas and humans."
Ānanda! After my parinirvāṇa, there will be a monastery named Nāḍika on Mount Urumuṇḍa in the city of Mathurā.

There, a bhikṣu named Bhadrika will appear, endowed with great supernormal powers and great majestic authority; he will have attained the Way through right wisdom, be learned and fearless, and uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā. He will instruct, exhort, benefit, and gladden those who practice the holy life, preaching the Dharma without weariness.
He, too, shall perform supernatural transformations and practice the holy life (brahmacarya), widely disseminating and propagating my True Dharma to increase the welfare of devas and humans.
"Ānanda!..."
"Do not grieve or lament.

After my parinirvāṇa, at the Nāṭika Monastery on Mount Uruvilvā, there will be a bhikṣu named Tiṣya, who possesses great supernormal powers and great majesty. He will tirelessly preach the Dharma to those practicing the holy life, enabling my teaching to be widely propagated and disseminated, thereby increasing the welfare of gods and humans."
Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be a mountain named Uśīra by the side of Mount Urubilvā.

There was an assembly of forty thousand bhikṣus who possessed supernormal powers and great majesty, were capable of much, had attained the Path through right knowledge, were learned and fearless, and were upholders of the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās; each was able to instruct, admonish, benefit, and gladden others in the holy life, preaching the Dharma without weariness.

Those bhikṣus, through their supernormal powers and transformations, shall practice the holy life so that my True Dharma may be widely propagated and disseminated, each being able to increase the assembly of devas and humans.
“Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament.

After my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Upagupta on the slopes of Mount Urumuṇḍa who possesses great supernormal powers and great majesty; he will even be able to perform miraculous transformations and practice the holy life, causing my True Dharma to be widely disseminated and spreading it so as to benefit devas and humans.”

In that place, there shall be a thousand arhats who, together with an assembly of eighty-eight thousand bhikṣus, shall perform a single poṣadha and carry out a single karmavācanā; being free from deceit in mind, they shall mutually bestow predictions upon one another.

They are all capable of supernatural transformations and practice the holy life (brahmacarya), causing my True Dharma to spread and circulate widely, each able to increase the assembly of devas and humans.

"Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament.

“Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament.

If I were to fully extol and describe in detail all the merits possessed by that Mātaṅga, I could not reach their end. Ānanda!
This bhikṣu Mātaṅga is endowed with all virtues; he is able to cause my Dharma, Vinaya, supernormal powers, and holy life to be widely practiced and disseminated among gods and humans.
“Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament.

By gradually accumulating the roots of goodness for awakening, after a full thousand kalpas in a future age, he will attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. "Do not grieve or lament.

In that place, there are many brahmins, elders, and householders who follow the sūtras and have deep faith in me and my śrāvakas; they make offerings to them, revere them, respect them, and praise them.
He has immeasurable śrāvaka disciples who possess great supernormal powers, are endowed with great majesty, and have extensive capabilities.
Ānanda! Among them, there are many elders and householders who have attained the Path through right knowledge, are learned and fearless, and are endowed with great wisdom.

"Could the True Dharma of the Buddha be on the verge of disappearing?"

"At that time, in the royal capital of Puṣkaravatī, there will be a lay follower (upāsaka) named Dharmavardhana, who possesses great supernormal powers, great majesty, and great merit; who has attained the Way through right wisdom, is widely learned and fearless, and is skilled in means as he upholds the Sūtras and Mātṛkās."

In order to inspire reverence and faith in those brahmins, householders, and lay devotees, this upāsaka ascended into the air and, demonstrating, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them, spoke these words:
"All of you, people, take care not to be afraid, do not doubt, and do not worry; the True Dharma of that Śākyamuni Buddha still abides in the world."

"You should exert diligent effort and perform various wholesome deeds, so that what has not been attained may be attained, what has not been realized may be realized, and what has not been reached may be reached."
"The Noble Dharma still exists now; you should seek it with haste.

At that time, the brahmins, householders, and lay devotees were all filled with joy in their hearts, and they practiced giving, performed various meritorious deeds, adorned and reverently maintained my relics, and diligently made offerings to the śrāvakas. Those brahmins, householders, and laypeople—for whom he taught, instructed, benefited, and gladdened through that Dharma—all proceeded upon the path of wholesome states and the path to nirvāṇa.
"Ānanda!
That upāsaka will also enable my True Dharma to be widely practiced and disseminated, increasing the welfare of devas and humans.
It is thus, Ānanda!"

After my parinirvāṇa, there will likewise be many laypeople who have attained deep faith and reverence within my Dharma—those who, in the past, made offerings to many hundreds, many thousands, and immeasurable Buddhas, and planted various roots of goodness—and who will diligently cultivate the adornment of my relics and offer worship, respect, honor, and praise to the śrāvakas.
"Ānanda! They, too, will cause my True Dharma to spread widely and be disseminated, increasing the welfare of devas and humans. Ānanda!"

After my parinirvāṇa, in a future age, there shall appear in the northern region of India a bhikṣu named Gopaka. Having planted roots of goodness under countless hundreds of Buddhas in the past, he has made offerings and shown them reverence; he is endowed with profound faith, dwells securely in the Mahāyāna, and has given rise to such a resolve out of a desire to have compassion for, benefit, and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings. He will be widely learned and uphold the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, extolling the Mahāyāna and elucidating the Mahāyāna.

When these bhikṣus see my relics, images, or stūpas that have fallen into ruin, they shall restore and repair them, adorning them with gold and erecting banners and streamers; they shall provide precious canopies and nets of bells that emit subtle and wondrous sounds.

They shall create immeasurable images of the Tathāgata and various stūpas and temples, all of which shall be adorned with half-moons and lions, thereby enabling the hearts of the multitudes of devas and humans to give rise to faith and joy.

In order to fulfill the roots of merit for enlightenment; out of compassion for sentient beings; to protect, sustain, and nurture them; to gather and uphold my Dharma; to cause those who lack reverence and faith to increase their reverence and faith through practice; and also to cause many multitudes to plant roots of goodness, one should perform the Pañcavārṣika assembly.

Ānanda! At that time, there will be many bhikṣus who do not uphold the prohibitions and precepts, who frequently act contrary to the Dharma, and who take no pleasure in secluded groves. They will abandon the joy of meditative concentration, break the precepts, and deviate from the Path. They will engage in mutual disputes and litigation, be greedily attached to accumulation, and monopolize single rooms for themselves. They will socialize with worldly people, abandon the Buddha-Dharma, show no reverence for the holy life (brahmacarya), and be mere semblances of śramaṇas.

At that time, there will be some bhikṣus who exert diligent effort, remain secluded from bustle, maintain mindfulness before them, and unify their minds through concentration and wisdom; they will dwell securely in wholesome dharmas, have few desires and be content, delight in the practice of alms-gathering, abide in the noble lineages, possess great learning and fearlessness, and uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās.
At that time, the bhikṣu Kevaddha caused those bhikṣus who wore the kaṣāya to have supple minds and unimpaired faculties, and to be endowed with profound faith and the highest reverence;

toward all those wearing the kaṣāya, he gave rise to the perception of them as upholders of the precepts and the perception of them as fields of merit, and thus practiced giving and cultivated various roots of goodness.

That bhikṣu Gopaka, having cultivated and accumulated immeasurable and various most excellent roots of merit for bodhi, passed away and was reborn in the Land of Immeasurable Life in the western direction, beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-worlds.

Having planted various roots of goodness under that Buddha and further practiced the holy life under eighty billion other Tathāgatas, he will, by virtue of these roots of goodness, attain perfect enlightenment after ninety-nine billion kalpas have passed in a future age; the Buddha’s name shall be Vimalaprabha, and the world shall be named Sarvaguṇavyūha.
"Ānanda! That bhikṣu Gopaka shall cause my true Dharma to be widely practiced and disseminated among devas and humans. Ānanda!"
"Do not grieve or lament.
My holy life shall spread widely, and gods and humans will have faith and joy in it, Ānanda!"
After my parinirvāṇa, in a future age, there shall be a frontier kingdom named Śama.
In that land there will be a king named Mahādāna, who will conceive pure faith in my Dharma and diligently practice offerings to my relics and my śrāvakas, extolling and praising them.

Ānanda! That King Mahādāna will assemble my community of śrāvaka bhikṣus in the kingdom of Śamā and honor them with offerings. Therein, there shall be more than three thousand arhats—all possessing supernormal powers, merit, and majestic authority, and who are untiring in preaching the Dharma for the sake of the holy life.
“Ānanda! They, too, will be able to cause my True Dharma to be widely practiced and disseminated among gods and humans. Ānanda!”
"Do not grieve or lament.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be a city named Kṣemavatī in the country of Northern India.

There they shall receive my relics and honor them with offerings of flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, sounds, music, banners, flags, jeweled parasols, robes, bedding, and various treasures such as gold and silver."
Ānanda! At that time, many people will leave the household life out of faith in that vihāra, upholding the prohibitive precepts and practicing wholesome dharmas;
likewise, the number of laypeople who practice wholesome dharmas will also be immeasurable.

Ānanda! There are those who uphold the precepts, possess great learning, and are wise; who have attained deep, pure faith within my Dharma; who diligently cultivate the adornment of my śrāvakas and my relics, performing their purification and offerings;
and who provide offerings and protection to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

Having received the retribution of merit among gods and humans through these roots of goodness, some shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, some shall attain the vehicle of the *pratyekabuddha*, and some shall attain the vehicle of the *śrāvaka* and enter *nirvāṇa*.
Ānanda! By means of such various offerings as these, they shall attain such supernormal powers and majestic authority. Ānanda!
These individuals shall reveal and expound [the teachings], causing my True Dharma to spread widely among gods and humans.
Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament.
"My True Dharma shall spread widely and increase the welfare of devas and humans. Ānanda!

My relics and my images will be found throughout Jambudvīpa; how much more so those images fashioned within the palaces of those who do not see me—namely, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth?"
"Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament; my Dharma and Vinaya shall be widely disseminated among gods and humans.
Chapter Seven: The Relics (Śarīra-varga) At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"After my parinirvāṇa, if there are sons or daughters of good family—whether lay or ordained—who offer even as much as a mustard seed of my relics, honoring, respecting, and making humble offerings to them;
I declare that by this root of goodness, all such persons shall attain the fruit of nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa."
Ānanda! After my parinirvāṇa, if there are sons or daughters of good family who give rise to reverent faith and construct images, stupas, or temples for me.

Ānanda! You should give rise to deep faith and be careful not to harbor doubts; I declare that by means of these roots of goodness, all such persons shall attain the fruit of nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.

Ānanda! Let alone those who currently make offerings to me; let alone those who, after my parinirvāṇa, make offerings to even as much as a mustard seed’s worth of my relics; let alone those who construct images of me and build stūpas and temples for me.

Ānanda! If there are those with faith who contemplate the merits of the Buddha and scatter even a single flower into the air, I declare that by this root of goodness, all such persons shall attain the fruit of nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.

Ānanda! If there are those who, having seen the supernatural power and majesty of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, scatter even a single flower into the air as an offering, they are still able to attain the fruit of nirvāṇa; how much more so for those who personally attend upon the Tathāgata to make offerings, or those who, after my parinirvāṇa, make offerings to my relics?
Ānanda! The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable; likewise, the merit obtained by anyone who is able to make offerings to it is also inconceivable.

Ānanda! If a person recollects the Buddha and even scatters a single flower into the air, I, with my Buddha-wisdom, perceive and know that the karmic fruit obtained by such a person is inconceivable; you should have faith in this.
"How much more so for all the sons of the Buddha in the future who have attained deep reverence and faith, who contemplate the merits of the Buddha, and who seek the wisdom of the Buddha?
At that time, having heard the Buddha's words, Ānanda was filled with exultation; giving rise to great joy, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How rare, Bhagavān!"
"How marvelous, Sugata!

Now is the very time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will explain the karmic fruit obtained by those who practice the recollection of the Buddha, even down to one who scatters a single flower into the air as an offering."
The bhikṣus shall obtain this by hearing it from the Buddha, reciting it, and upholding it.

Out of compassion for the world and for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of gods and humans, all sentient beings in the present and future worlds who hear it from them shall, in turn, repeatedly cultivate various roots of goodness; their hearts will give rise to reverent faith, and they will attain great satisfaction.
He thought to himself:
"Śākyamuni, the unsurpassed Dharma King among the Śākyas, the Greatly Compassionate One who pities the world, has exhorted us, causing us to give rise to mindfulness and exert great diligence."
After he had spoken these words, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall analyze and explain for you the karmic retributions that are obtained."
Ānanda said: "So be it, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there are sentient beings who, because they have practiced mindfulness of the Buddha, scatter even a single flower into the air, the karmic fruit and retribution obtained from such merit will be inexhaustible."

Ānanda! Thus, as for these sentient beings who have come from the past—through kalpas of vast duration and the wandering of birth and death—their beginning cannot be known; it is likewise so regarding the future limit.

If there are sentient beings who, with a mind of utmost sincerity, recollect the merits of the Buddha and even scatter a single flower into the air, they shall in future ages attain the status of Śakra-devānām-indra, Brahmā-devānām-indra, or a Cakravartin King;
their meritorious rewards will likewise be inexhaustible. Because the limits of their roots of goodness and karmic rewards cannot be exhausted, they must ultimately enter parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Ānanda!
The field of merit that is the Buddha cannot be exhausted by the fruits of conditioned existence; I say that such a person will certainly attain nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.

“Ānanda! Let alone those who have personally attended upon and made offerings to me; let alone those who have made offerings to my relics, even as small as a mustard seed; let alone those who have constructed images of me and various stūpas and temples to make offerings; let alone those who, out of mindfulness of the Buddha, have made offerings by scattering even a single flower into the air.
Furthermore, Ānanda, if there is anyone who, while inside a room, scatters even a single flower into the air out of mindfulness of the Buddha,

I declare that this person shall attain nirvāṇa— the supreme nirvāṇa, the nirvāṇa that reaches its ultimate limit, the most excellent nirvāṇa, the wondrous nirvāṇa, the pure nirvāṇa, and the nirvāṇa in which they dwell securely.
Ānanda! For these reasons, among all fields of merit, the Buddha is the foremost; the Buddha is the king. Why is this so?
As for making offerings to the Buddha-field, it cannot be fully exhausted by worldly karmic retribution;
for this reason, the Buddha-field is the most supreme among all fields of merit.

Ānanda! The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas—who follow the true path—are able to serve as the unsurpassed, ultimate field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). For all those who give to this field of merit that is the Buddha, they will surely reach the limit of *nirvāṇa* and attain the foremost *nirvāṇa*.

“Ānanda! Let alone the merit obtained by scattering flowers upon the Buddha as just described; if there is another person who merely brings the Buddha to mind with a heart of reverence and faith for even a single lifetime, I declare that this person shall likewise attain the fruit of nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.”

Ānanda! Let alone the merit of recollecting the Buddha among human beings; if even an animal should be able to give rise to such recollection toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, I declare that its roots of goodness and karmic rewards shall lead it to attain nirvāṇa and reach the very limit of nirvāṇa.

Ānanda! You should now observe that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, who act as fields of merit for all sentient beings, are able to cause sentient beings to attain such supernormal powers and majestic authority.
Therefore, Ānanda, do not grieve or lament.

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family, even down to animals— all such sentient beings— who conceive faith in the Buddha, they shall attain such fruits of supernatural power and vast merit, which are like nectar— the foremost nectar that reaches the very limit of nectar.

“Ānanda! You have served the Tathāgata with physical and verbal kindness and filial piety, providing immeasurable peace and happiness; your mind is without duality, free from anger, free from resentment, and free from enmity.”
Ānanda! Suppose this trichiliocosm were filled with stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and arhats, as dense as a grove of sugarcane, bamboo, hemp, or grass.
If there are good men or good women who, for an eon or slightly less than an eon, with all manner of pleasing articles of enjoyment, respectfully honor, revere, and humbly make offerings [to them].
Ānanda! What do you think?
Is the merit obtained by these sons and daughters of good family not indeed great?
Ānanda said:
“Very much, Blessed One! Very much, Sugata!”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

If there were another person who, in the presence of the Buddhas, were to join their palms but once or utter the name [of the Buddha] but once, the merit of this would not equal even a hundredth part of the former merit; it would not equal a thousandth part, nor a hundred-thousand-billionth part, nor any numerical fraction, nor any fraction of a *kalā*. It would not equal even a single *kalā*.”
Why is this? Ānanda!
Because among all fields of merit, the Buddha-Tathāgata is the most supreme; therefore, making offerings to the Buddha brings about great merit, spiritual powers, and majestic authority.

“Ānanda! Let alone all the śrāvakas, arhats, and so forth who exist throughout the trichiliocosm; suppose, moreover, that the trichiliocosm were filled with pratyekabuddhas, as dense as a field of sugarcane, bamboo, hemp, or grass.”

If there are good sons or good daughters who, for one kalpa or slightly less than a kalpa, honor, revere, and humbly make offerings to those pratyekabuddhas with all manner of pleasing articles of enjoyment.

If, after the parinirvāṇa of a pratyekabuddha, a stūpa made of the seven precious jewels is erected, and if some son or daughter of good family, for as long as they live, reverently honors, respects, and humbly makes offerings to it with various incense flowers, unguents, powdered incense, robes, bedding, jeweled banners, flags, and canopies;
Ānanda! What do you think?
Would the merit obtained by that person be great indeed?
Ānanda said:
“Very many, Blessed One! Very many, Sugata!”
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
Suppose there is another person who, toward the Tathāgata, gives rise to a single thought of pure faith, reflection, and resolute belief, and speaks these words:”
"The wisdom of all Buddhas is inconceivable.

By means of the roots of goodness and merit derived from this faith and understanding, compared to the merit previously obtained from making offerings to those pratyekabuddhas, it does not approach even a *kalā* part of it, nor even a *upaniṣad* part of it.
Why is this? Ānanda!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess immeasurable great kindness, immeasurable great compassion, immeasurable precepts, immeasurable concentration, immeasurable wisdom, immeasurable liberation, immeasurable knowledge and vision of liberation, immeasurable cultivation and accumulation, and immeasurable realization and verification.

Ānanda! The wisdom of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is inconceivable, and the realm of the Buddhas is also inconceivable; if one makes offerings to that which is inconceivable, one shall obtain an inconceivable reward.
“Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament; you shall obtain the merit and benefits of great supernormal powers. Why is this?

Ānanda! For more than twenty years you have served me with loving-kindness through body, speech, and mind. You have received and upheld the eighty-four thousand clusters of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-treasures; among those of great learning you are foremost, being preeminent in eloquence, wisdom, and skill in answering questions. Having attained the Way through right knowledge, you possess vast learning and fearlessness. You uphold the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā, preaching the Dharma to the fourfold assembly without weariness.
Ānanda! After my parinirvāṇa, you and the venerable Mahākāśyapa shall act as the foremost and greatest teachers, performing great deeds of the Buddha.
"Ānanda! Do not grieve or lament; you shall attain the merit, benefits, and great supernormal powers.

"If there are sentient beings who hear the name of the Buddha, I declare that such persons will certainly and surely attain entry into parinirvāṇa."
“Ānanda! If there is someone who utters the words ‘Namo Buddha,’ what is the meaning of this?

Excellent, World-Honored One!”
“I pray that you will explain this meaning for the sake of the bhikṣus, so that I may now personally receive, hear, and uphold it.

“I wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! What is called ‘Namo Buddha’ is the definitive sound of the name of all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Ānanda!”
Because these names, sounds, and meanings of the Buddhas are definitive, one proclaims, "Namo to all Buddhas. Ānanda!

For this reason, I shall speak a parable so that all sentient beings may increase their faith in this Dharma, and so that all good sons and good daughters, upon hearing the names and sounds of the Buddha-Bhagavāns, may attain profound reverence and faith.

“Ānanda! Once in the past, there was a great caravan leader who led a multitude of merchants into the great ocean. Having reached that sea, their ship was suddenly seized by a makara, a great fish, which intended to swallow it.
"Ānanda!

At that time, the caravan leader and the merchants were struck with terror, their hair standing on end; they were filled with grief and distress, fearing they would not survive. Without rescue, without protection, without refuge, and without a resort, each wept bitterly, wailed, lamented, and repented, uttering various cries of sorrow:
'Alas, what a tragedy!'"
"This Jambudvīpa is thus delightful and thus rare; human existence in this world is thus difficult to obtain.
Now I shall be separated from my parents; I shall be parted from my brothers, sisters, wife, children, kinsmen, and friends.
I shall no longer see them, nor shall I be able to see the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha."
They wept with extreme great compassion, sorrowful and unhappy, each praying to various honored deities and heavenly beings in their desire to seek their own deliverance. “Ānanda!

At that time, the caravan leader was one of right view with far-reaching clarity; his mind had attained pure faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and he no longer placed his trust in any other celestial deities.”
At that time, the merchant leader addressed the merchants:
"Gentlemen, you should know that if you wish to survive, escape this peril, and attain liberation, you must all speak with one voice simultaneously according to what I say;
even if we do not attain liberation in this life, we shall be reborn in a good realm in a future existence."
When those merchants heard these words, they each said to the caravan leader, "We shall follow your instructions;
we only pray that you will speak quickly.
"Ānanda! [he replied.]

At that time, the merchant leader bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and remained upon the ship, single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha. With palms joined in prostration, he cried out in a loud voice:
"Namo to all Buddhas!"
"O you who have attained great fearlessness, O you of great compassion, O you who pity all sentient beings!
Thus he spoke three times.
At that moment, the merchants also simultaneously joined their palms in prostration and, with one voice and in unison, cried out:
"Homage to all Buddhas!
To those who bestow fearlessness, the Greatly Compassionate Ones, who have pity for all sentient beings.
Thus he recited this three times.

At that time, upon hearing the name of the Buddha and the sound of his prostrations, that makara fish conceived great love and reverence, attained a mind free from the intent to kill, and immediately closed its mouth as soon as it heard him.

“Ānanda! At that time, the merchant leader and all the merchants were entirely safe and sound, having escaped the peril of the fish; their ship and the merchants’ wishes were fulfilled, and they returned safely to Jambudvīpa.”
At that time, upon hearing the Buddha’s voice, the makara fish felt joy and happiness in his heart; he ceased eating other sentient beings and died as a result.
Having passed away, he was reborn among human beings.
Once born among humans, he heard the Dharma and Vinaya from that Buddha, attained profound pure faith, and left the household life to become a renunciant.

Having gone forth, he drew near to virtuous friends; through humble service and offerings, he attained the path of Arhatship, became endowed with the six supernormal powers, and entered parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.

“Ānanda! Behold that fish who, having been born in the realm of animals, heard the name of the Buddha; having heard the name of the Buddha, he was reborn in the human realm; by virtue of being born in the human realm, he was able to go forth into homelessness; having gone forth, he immediately attained the fruit of arhatship; and having attained arhatship, he entered parinirvāṇa.”
Ānanda! Observe how such is the supernatural power of the Buddhas.
Having heard it, those fish will obtain supernormal powers, renown and fame, and their benefit will be certain.

How much more so for those who hear the name of the Buddha, listen to the True Dharma, and personally attend upon the Buddha to plant various roots of goodness—how could they not certainly attain benefit?

“Ānanda! As I have said in the past, by performing a small root of goodness one obtains a small portion of retribution; by fulfilling a complete root of goodness one obtains a complete portion of retribution. Ānanda!”

Regarding what is called "a small portion of roots of goodness": because such a person desires to reach maturity quickly, they plant the seeds of a śrāvaka and practice the Śrāvaka Vehicle, whereby through these roots of goodness they fulfill the stage of a śrāvaka;
or they plant the seeds of a pratyekabuddha and practice the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, whereby through these roots of goodness they fulfill the stage of a pratyekabuddha.
"Ānanda! For these reasons, I speak of the practice of limited cultivation. Ānanda!"

Regarding those who practice the path of fulfillment: these individuals have, from time immemorial, planted the seeds of Buddhahood in the presence of various Buddhas and cultivated all roots of goodness over a vast duration. By the power of the causes and conditions of these roots of goodness, they encounter the Buddhas;
having encountered the Buddhas, they do so for the sake of accumulating and fulfilling the roots of goodness that constitute enlightenment;

and having fulfilled these roots of goodness for enlightenment, they attain the Buddha-way—namely, becoming a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose voice resounds throughout the world. This is called the path of fulfillment.
Ānanda! This practice of complete fulfillment has already been explained at length by me in various sūtras in the past.
You should understand this sequence: if one practices with limited portions, one obtains limited results; if one practices with complete fulfillment, one obtains complete results.

“Ānanda! As it is also stated in my sūtras, ‘[Even] up to the point of receiving and upholding as few as four lines of verse,’ such statements were made by me according to what was appropriate for the sake of sentient beings who have dull faculties, meager merit, and little wisdom.”

“Ānanda! For all sentient beings who have no refuge, I act as their refuge; for those who have no shelter, I act as their dwelling; for those who have no protector, I act as their protection; for those who are ignorant, I act as their lamp of light; and for those who are blind and sightless, I act as their eyes.”
Ānanda! All those outside the Way, who are deluded, ignorant, and lacking wisdom, cannot save themselves; how then could they save others as their true refuge? Ānanda!
I am the teacher of all devas and humans, one who has compassion for all sentient beings.

In the future age when the Dharma is about to perish, there will be bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who, having gone forth within my Dharma, shall walk about hand-in-hand with their children, going from tavern to tavern and practicing unchaste conduct within my Dharma.
"Although they were motivated by the cause of wine, all of them shall attain parinirvāṇa within this Bhadrakalpa.
Ānanda! For what reason is it called the 'Auspicious Kalpa' (Bhadrakalpa)?"
Ānanda! When this trichiliocosm is about to be formed at the end of a kalpa, it becomes entirely one vast body of water.

At that time, a deity from the Śuddhāvāsa heavens observes this world with his divine eye and sees only this single great expanse of water. He sees a thousand exquisite lotus flowers—each lotus having a thousand petals, golden in color, with golden light shining forth in brilliant radiance, and their fragrance so pervasive and delightful as to be truly enchanting. Having seen this, the deity of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens feels immeasurable joy and exultation, and he proclaims in praise:
"How marvelous, how marvelous!
How rare, how rare!
Within this kalpa, one thousand Buddhas shall appear in the world."
For these reasons, this eon was consequently named Bhadra-kalpa, the "Auspicious Eon. Ānanda!

After my parinirvāṇa, within this Bhadra-kalpa, nine hundred and ninety-six Buddhas shall appear in the world—beginning with Tathāgata Krakucchanda and with me as the fourth; thereafter, Maitreya shall succeed me, continuing in this sequence until the final Tathāgata Roca. You should know this succession.

“Ānanda! Within my Dharma, there may even be those who, though their nature makes them defilers of the conduct of a śramaṇa, call themselves śramaṇas and resemble śramaṇas in appearance, and who wear the saṃghāṭī robe.”

In this Bhadrakalpa—from Maitreya as the foremost down to the final Tathāgata Roca—all those śramaṇas shall, in the presence of these Buddhas, sequentially attain parinirvāṇa in the realm of nirvana without remainder, leaving nothing behind.
Why is this so? Ānanda!
Among all such śramaṇas, even those who have uttered the name of the Buddha but once or given rise to faith for a single moment, the merit they have created shall never be in vain.
“Ānanda! By means of my buddha-wisdom, I measure and know the dharma-realm; it is not that I do not measure and know it. Ānanda!”
All white karma results in white retribution, and black karma results in black retribution.
Ānanda, if there are sentient beings with pure minds who utter these words of praise, "Namo Buddha," [they shall likewise receive such fruit].
Such a person, by virtue of these roots of goodness, will certainly attain nirvana and draw near to it; with a continuous flow, they shall enter the realm of nirvana.

How much more so for those who encounter a Buddha living in the world and personally receive him with reverence, humbly welcoming and seeing him off, honoring and making offerings to him, as well as those who, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, make offerings to his relics?

Ānanda! Those who are by nature defiled and dishonorable toward śramaṇas, yet claim to be śramaṇas and merely resemble śramaṇas in appearance—even such individuals should at least utter the name of the Buddha once; how much more so those whose minds can give rise to respectful faith and plant various roots of goodness?
Ānanda! For this reason, I have spoken these verses:
"The Buddhas are thus inconceivable, And the True Dharma of the Buddhas is likewise."
If one can reverently believe in the inconceivable, one will surely obtain inconceivable retribution.
All Tathāgatas of the past, who were able to manifest light and compassion, also once made offerings to the Buddha Mahāsthāmaprāpta;
those who awakened to supreme bodhi are beyond counting.
In the past, I was always in accord with generosity, Bestowing gifts out of compassion to rescue all sentient beings.
With roots of pure faith deep and diligent vigor, I transformed all things through that diligent vigor;
I cherished and honored sentient beings as I do my parents, My brothers, my relatives, and all my kinsmen.
Free from anger and resentment toward all kinsmen, I have awakened to the peerless Bodhi that is beyond counting.
When I sought the bliss of Bodhi, I practiced giving throughout immeasurable kalpas;
out of compassion and pity for sentient beings, I relinquished my body, head, eyes, flesh, and blood.
He also renounced immeasurable, heavy royal thrones, beloved wives, concubines, and children,
as well as countless precious vehicles, elephants, and horse-drawn chariots, for the sake of seeking supreme enlightenment;
throughout immeasurable thousands of millions of billions of eons, he repeatedly exerted himself with diligence and ran forward.
With a pure mind, they practice immeasurable generosity for the sake of seeking this supreme enlightenment;
They endure immeasurable sufferings and afflictions— ice, cold, poison, heat, hunger, and thirst—
and exert diligent effort without abandoning it until death for the sake of seeking the most excellent enlightenment.
Even if I were to speak for a hundred years or an eon, I could never exhaustively describe the characteristics of his conduct;
it is out of compassion for all sentient beings that he seeks the supreme enlightenment of peace and bliss.
Throughout the cycle of birth and death, they constantly encounter hundreds of billions of Tathāgatas;
to those Tathāgatas of great power, they constantly offer golden flowers,
as well as delicacies, food and drink, and clothing, along with ointments, powdered incense, and various flower garlands.
With many billions of jeweled banners, supreme pennants, and canopies, I made offerings to all such Tathāgatas.
Countless billions of sentient beings, Wandering through birth and death without end—
I constantly went to them to offer comfort, And through supreme generosity, widely benefited all multitudes.
Ethical discipline, patience, and diligent vigor; Meditative concentration, samādhi, wisdom, and skillful means;
The applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, And the well-cultivated practice of the four bases of power;
Likewise cultivating the five faculties and the five powers, The seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path.
I cultivate all factors conducive to enlightenment, for the sake of seeking this supreme bodhi.
With right wisdom I perform all actions; there is not a single unwholesome deed among them.
Constantly practicing all conduct with heedfulness, I have never committed even a hair’s breadth of fault or evil.
Chapter Nine: The Roots of Goodness The Mahākaruṇā-sūtra, Chapter Nine: The Roots of Goodness At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

“If there are sentient beings who give rise to even a single thought of faith toward the Buddhas, such roots of goodness will never perish; how much more so for those who perform other various roots of goodness?”
Ānanda! For the sake of making the meaning known to sentient beings, I employ parables; for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables.
"Ānanda! [he said].
It is as if, for example, someone were to split a single hair into a hundred parts, take one part of that hair to moisten a single drop of water, and bring it to me, saying:
"Gautama!..."

"I entrust this water to you, Gautama; do not let it increase or decrease. Furthermore, do not allow the wind or sun to blow upon or scorch it until it dries up or is exhausted. Do not let birds or beasts drink it all away. Do not allow other waters to mix with it. Carry it supported in a vessel; do not set it on the ground."
The Tathāgata then accepted that entrustment;
having accepted it, he placed it in the Ganges River, neither allowing it to swirl back nor permitting other objects to rub against or strike it.

In this way, a drop of water enters a great river and flows along with the current; it does not enter eddies, nor does it encounter any obstruction, and it is not entirely consumed by birds or beasts.
In this way, the drop of water neither increases nor decreases, remaining exactly as it was before, yet together with the great mass of water, it gradually enters the great ocean.
If that drop of water were to remain for an eon when the Vairambha winds arise and destroy the world-system, I too would likewise remain for an eon.
At that time, when the kalpa has come to an end, that person will come to me and say:
"Gautama! I previously deposited water with you; does it still exist now?"

"Ānanda! At that time, the Tathāgata knows and perceives the location of that drop of water within the great ocean; it is not mixed with other waters, it neither increases nor decreases, and it remains as it was, equal as before. He then takes it back and returns it to that person."

“Ānanda! Thus it is that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses great supernormal powers, great majesty, and great capability; he possesses pure great wisdom, immeasurable wisdom, and unimpeded knowledge and vision. In such matters as these, he is clear and unobstructed, being the most honored and the most supreme among those entrusted with a deposit.”
If one entrusts such a minute drop of water to the Buddha, it will not diminish or be lost even after a vast period of time.
Ānanda, you should understand this meaning!
The fine tip of a hair is a metaphor for the mind, intellect, and consciousness;
the Ganges River is a metaphor for the stream of birth and death;
and a single drop of water is a metaphor for a single instance of generating the resolve [for enlightenment] and its slight roots of goodness.
The great ocean is a metaphor for the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha;
the person to whom it is entrusted is a metaphor for those faithful Brahmins, elders, and householders;

and dwelling for one kalpa is a metaphor for the Buddha, the Tathāgata, who accepts that entrusted water and never lets it diminish, just as that person’s entrusted drop of water remains without losing even a hair’s breadth throughout the vast expanse of time.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
If one has produced even a single thought of faith toward the Buddha, that root of goodness will not be lost; how much more so for other superior and sublime roots of goodness?
I declare that all such persons are destined for the fruit of nirvāṇa, reaching even unto the very limit of nirvāṇa.

“Ānanda! Suppose there were someone who, having encountered the Tathāgata, gave rise to a single thought of resolve and developed a lifetime of reverent faith; yet, due to the obstruction of other unwholesome and evil karmas, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts—this is because they must experience for themselves the karma they have created.”

If the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, endowed with great compassion, appear in the world, they know through unobstructed wisdom that these sentient beings originally cultivated roots of goodness, yet have fallen into hell due to the obstruction of other unwholesome and evil karmas.
Having known this, the Buddha pulls them out from that hell and establishes them on the shore in a place free from fear.
Having established them on the shore, he further causes those sentient beings to recollect the wholesome deeds they performed in the past, and instructs them, saying:
"O sons of good family!..."

You all should recollect the roots of goodness you planted in the past—roots of goodness such as these, which were cultivated and sown at a certain time, in a certain world, and in the presence of a certain Buddha.
Those people, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic authority, immediately regained their memory;
having regained it, they spoke these words: "So it is, Bhagavān!"
"So it is, Sugata!
The Buddha spoke again, saying: "Good son!

The small roots of goodness you have previously planted in the presence of the Tathāgatas remain unimpaired and undiminished; from them you shall obtain benefit—namely, the cessation of all suffering and the attainment of all happiness.
"Good son! That you have come here is the realm of the Buddha.

Throughout the long night, you have wandered through birth and death within a sphere that is not your proper domain; yet, from time immemorial, the small roots of goodness you have planted in the presence of the Buddhas have never been diminished."

It is, for example, like a prince, a king, or a high minister who, having committed some offense and being imprisoned, is released and set free after being exhorted to repent through the recounting of past events.
"In this way, Ānanda!

Those sentient beings, having originally planted roots of goodness with the Tathāgata, may—due to having committed other evil and unwholesome karmas—fall into the various evil realms such as the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts."

If the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, endowed with great compassion, appear in the world, they perceive and know all those who have been sustained by the causal conditions of the roots of goodness from their initial resolve; the Buddhas pull them out from within the hells and establish them upon the cool shore of Nirvana, in a place free from fear.
Having established them in a state of fearlessness, he causes them to recollect and instructs them, saying:
"Good sons! You should recollect that you have obtained such a reward through the causal conditions of the roots of goodness you previously cultivated."
Those sentient beings spoke thus: "So it is, Bhagavān! So it is, Sugata!"
"Because we have received the empowerment of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, we thus remember and know this.
Chapter Ten: The Merit of Giving and Virtue. *The Sutra of Great Compassion*, Chapter Ten: The Merit of Giving and Virtue. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"You should know that for such people as these, even the cultivation of minor roots of goodness is never in vain. Even those who give rise to a single thought of faith—I declare that all such persons shall attain nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa."

For this reason, I have employed this analogy so that faithful men and women may attain profound pure faith, and further come to revere and respect [the teaching], giving rise to great love and joy, leaping for gladness.
“Ānanda! Just as a fisherman, in order to catch fish, places baited hooks in a large pond so that the fish may swallow them;
once the fish have swallowed the bait, although they remain in the pond, they will soon emerge.”
Why is this? Because when fish such as these are struck by those firm hooks and lines, although they remain in the water, you should know that these fish are effectively already on the shore.
Why is this? Because the hook and line were tied to a tree on the bank.
When the fisherman arrived at that place, he immediately knew he had caught a fish; he then pulled the hook and line onto the bank and used them as he pleased.
"In this way, Ānanda!

All sentient beings who have conceived respectful faith toward the Buddhas, planted various roots of goodness, and practiced generosity—even down to those who have resolved their minds and gained a single thought of faith—though they may be obscured and hindered by other evil and unwholesome karmas such that they fall into the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, and other places of hardship."

If a Buddha, the World-Honored One, appears in the world, he perceives with his Buddha-eye all sentient beings who practice the Bodhisattva vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Śrāvaka vehicle; he sees that these sentient beings have planted various roots of goodness, while these other sentient beings have severed their roots of goodness;
he sees that these sentient beings belong to the category of decline, while these others belong to the category of superior progress;

and he sees that these sentient beings plant various seeds in the ground of the noble ones, making offerings to the field of merit of the Buddhas, and even giving rise to a single moment of reverent faith and practicing generosity throughout their lives.

By virtue of these roots of goodness, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perceive with their Buddha-eye that this sentient being’s resolve is superior; they therefore pull them out from the hells and cause them to emerge.
Having pulled them out, they place them on the shore of nirvāṇa.
Once placed in nirvāṇa, they cause them to remember that they originally planted various roots of goodness under such-and-such a Buddha.
Having recollected this, he spoke these words:
"So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!"
The Buddha said,
“Sons of good family!
By means of these roots of goodness, you shall obtain great retribution and great benefit, because you have practiced giving and planted roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddha.”
"Good son!

Such a deposit shall never be lost; even after a vast duration of time, up to hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, that single root of goodness will surely lead to nirvana and reach the very limit of nirvana."

“Ānanda! What is called ‘fish’ is a metaphor for all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); the ‘pond’ is a metaphor for the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); the ‘hook’ is a metaphor for a single root of goodness planted by the Buddha; the ‘line’ is a metaphor for the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*); the ‘fisherman’ is a metaphor for the Buddha, the Tathāgata; and ‘using the fish as one pleases’ is a metaphor for all Tathāgatas establishing sentient beings in the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Ānanda! You should understand this sequence:

if one makes an offering to the field of the Buddha, even after a vast period of time, it will never perish, it will never be exhausted, and it will have no limit; it will certainly lead to the fruit of nirvāṇa.
“Ānanda! I shall now provide another simile: by making an offering to the field of the Buddha, one attains the foremost nirvāṇa, reaching the very limit of nirvāṇa. Ānanda!”

If there are sentient beings who crave worldly retribution, engage in worldly conduct, delight in the world, and long for the world, they practice generosity toward the Buddhas and dedicate these roots of goodness with the hope of attaining the good realms of humans and devas.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, having planted various roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddhas, speak thus:
"By these roots of goodness, I vow that in every lifetime I shall not enter nirvana."
"Ānanda! It is impossible that these sentient beings, by virtue of this root of goodness, would not enter nirvāṇa. Why is that?"

Ānanda! Such is the unsurpassed field of merit of the Buddhas—a field free from all desolation and impurity, devoid of thorns, transcending the stains and faults of desire, and exceedingly pure. If one plants even a small seed of roots of goodness and merit within such a field, it will not grow in other fields; yet in this field, it can serve as a seed for the three types of enlightenment: whether it be unsurpassed enlightenment, the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha, or the enlightenment of a śrāvaka.

Those roots of goodness will never be lost; because they have given rise to reverent faith through this act of giving, by virtue of these superior causes and conditions, they shall proceed toward the wholesome paths and pure dharmas, and will certainly enter nirvāṇa.

“Ānanda! It is, for example, as when an elder cultivates a field: the ground is not overgrown or desolate; it is free of thorns, brambles, tiles, and rubble; the soil is rich and fertile, having been tilled and made pliant.”

Taking fresh seeds and placing them in precious vessels so that they do not rot or decay, one plants them in the fields according to the proper seasons, irrigating, weeding, and tending to them at the appropriate times, always carefully protecting and maintaining them at all times.
Ānanda! Suppose that at another time, this householder who manages the fields goes to the field site and stands by the edge of the field, saying these words: "Alas, seed!"
"Do not plant, do not produce, and do not grow; I seek neither profit nor reward.
Ānanda, what do you think?
"Is it because one speaks with a farmer that the seed will not grow and will not function as a seed?
Ānanda replied, "No, Bhagavān!"
"No, Sugata! That will certainly produce fruit; it cannot be without a result.
The Buddha said:
"So it is, so it is, Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who,
while being attached to birth, death, and the fruits of craving within the three realms of existence, plant roots of goodness in the Buddha-field of merit, they shall speak thus:"
"By these roots of goodness, I vow that I shall not enter parinirvāṇa.
Ānanda! That such a person would not enter nirvāṇa is impossible.

Ānanda! Although such a person may not seek nirvāṇa with delight, because they have planted various roots of goodness under the Buddha, I declare that this person will certainly attain nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.

This applies even to those who, having encountered a Buddha, have produced a single thought of awakening or cultivated roots of goodness through a single moment of respectful faith; all such individuals shall attain parinirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.

“Ānanda! In future ages there will be kings of border regions who, though they do not understand the merit of the Buddha-dharma, will give rise to faith upon seeing a Buddhist vihāra or an image of the Buddha. When I was formerly taking birth in various places throughout the five realms of existence and practicing all the bodhisattva deeds, I gathered those border kings through the four methods of attraction: giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation.”

Ānanda! When that king of the borderland sees my vihāra and my image, he will give rise to a heart of reverent faith; by this root of goodness, he will surely attain nirvāṇa and reach the very limit of nirvāṇa.

Ānanda! Those frontier kings shall have ministers, princes, high officials, assistants, kinsmen and blood relations, as well as companions. After my parinirvāṇa, they shall see my vihāras and my images. Although they do not understand the merits of the Buddhas or the true Dharma of the Buddha, yet having cultivated few roots of goodness and having given rise to faith in me—whom I, while originally practicing the bodhisattva path, also sustained by means of the four methods of attraction (saṃgrahavastu)—by the empowerment of these roots of goodness, they shall attain nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.
Ānanda! Throughout the long night, out of compassion for sentient beings, I have gathered them in through the four means of attraction and nurtured them with the benefit of all Buddha-dharmas.

“Ānanda! Observe how when the Tathāgata walks along the road, he causes the high places of the great earth to become low and the low places to become high, so that all uneven elevations and depressions become perfectly level; yet once the Tathāgata has passed, the ground immediately returns to its original state.

All the trees and forests lean toward the Buddha, and the tree deities manifest their forms to bow their heads in prostration; yet once the Tathāgata has passed, the trees immediately return to their original positions.”

Hills, mounds, pits, latrines, filth, thorns, thickets, and all manner of rubble were entirely cleared away; the ground was leveled and made even, pure and free from impurity, fragrant and intensely aromatic, most delightful to behold, with various flowers strewn upon the earth, magnificent and radiant, over which the Tathāgata walked as he passed.

Ānanda! Behold the various meritorious virtues of all the wholesome deeds practiced by the Tathāgata in the past: when he traveled along the road, there was no sentient being who did not bow down and prostrate themselves; even insentient things—the great earth, mountain cliffs, forests, and medicinal herbs—did not fail to incline and bend where the Buddha walked.
Why is this? Ānanda!

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I bowed down in prostration before all my teachers; I also bowed down in prostration with the utmost reverence toward my father and mother. Toward elders, seniors, those of middle age, the young, and my own kinsmen and blood relations, there were none before whom I did not bow down. This included the Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even non-Buddhist seers possessing the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā), as well as śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—all such persons worthy of receiving offerings.

To all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, non-Buddhist sages, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, parents, brothers, kinsmen, and blood relations, as well as other elders, middle-aged persons, youths, and fellow disciples under the same teacher—to all these, one should incline, humble oneself, and pay respectful homage.

Ānanda! By virtue of the retribution of such wholesome karma, once I have attained Buddhahood in unsurpassed bodhi, all those things—both sentient and insentient—will incline, bow their heads, and pay homage whenever the Tathāgata walks by.
“Ānanda! In the past, I have indeed—with a sincere heart and with my own hands—given pure, exquisite, and pleasing assets to my teachers and other sentient beings.”
Ānanda! By virtue of this karmic retribution, when the Tathāgata walks, the great earth becomes level and even, swept and cleansed, pure and free of mud, and moreover devoid of tiles and pebbles.

“Ānanda! In the presence of immeasurable Tathāgatas, when Bodhisattvas, kinsmen, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhist sages were traveling along the road, I in the past have swept and cleared the paths and plastered their dwellings.”

Whether walking or staying within the Buddha’s vihāra, I shall sweep and clean it with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of equanimity, a mind free from pride or inferiority, a mind free from deceit, and a pure mind; at all times, I shall constantly seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi for the sake of all sentient beings, for the peace and happiness of all sentient beings, out of compassion for all sentient beings, and for the benefit, peace, and happiness of all devas and humans.

Ānanda! By virtue of these roots of goodness, wherever the Buddha-Tathāgata may be—whether walking, standing, sitting, or reflecting with the intention to come or go—the streets and alleys at the head of his path will naturally become pure, and the ground will be level as the palm of a hand.
"Ānanda! All the merits of the Tathāgata’s bodily actions are so preeminent and difficult to comprehend that their limit cannot be reached. Ānanda!"

Now, in order to fulfill this purpose, there shall be faithful sons and daughters of good family who will conceive profound reverence and faith toward the Tathāgata, attaining what they have never experienced before.
Ānanda! Sumeru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas high, and it is likewise eighty-four thousand yojanas deep within the great ocean. Ānanda!
Even when I enter parinirvāṇa, this firm and lofty king of mountains would not fail to lean and topple; how much more so the other Black Mountains, medicinal herbs, and groves?
If they were not to lean over, it would be impossible. "Ānanda!

Setting aside the firm Sumeru, King of Mountains, even all the Cakravāḍa mountains—sixteen thousand eight hundred yojanas high, and as firm as vajra—will, at the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, not fail to lean over and bow their heads in reverent salutation."
If one wishes to avoid it from afar so as not to lean or tilt toward it, that too is impossible.
Why is this? Ānanda!
When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I never abandoned any sentient beings in their various undertakings.
If there were sentient beings who were angry or discordant, I caused them to reconcile;

those who were formerly at odds, I was able to bring together, establishing them firmly and securely so that they remained intact and complete, each giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion.
Ānanda! By the power of these roots of goodness and their causal conditions, the Tathāgata has attained an indestructible body, and he also causes his retinue to be firm and unbreakable.

“Ānanda! The Tathāgata has further attained the quality of having a firm and indestructible retinue, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path.”

Ānanda! These thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are the great retinue of the Buddha-Tathāgata; all Buddhas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas dwell within them, and they cannot be destroyed by any beings among the devas and humans in all the worlds.
Why is this? Ānanda!

By means of this Dharma, when the Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, all those in the world—gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and their retinues; devas, humans, and asuras; as well as Mount Sumeru, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, the great earth, and all grasses and trees—will not fail to bow their heads and incline toward him. How, then, could anyone destroy it?
If there were anyone who could destroy it, such a thing is impossible.
Why is this? Ānanda!
“The body of the Tathāgata cannot be destroyed, nor can the relics of the Buddha be destroyed. Ānanda!

Out of compassion for all sentient beings and by virtue of his original vow, the Tathāgata has shattered these relics into pieces like mustard seeds, so that the Buddha-dharma may increase and spread far and wide.”
Ānanda! When the Tathāgata was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this vow:
"Once I have attained perfect enlightenment in anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and entered parinirvāṇa, may my śarīra be widely propagated."
"Ānanda! By virtue of my original vow, after my parinirvāṇa, I shall cause these śarīras to increase and spread far and wide.
Those sentient beings, by beholding the Buddha-Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, shall attain the fruits of the noble path."
Out of compassion for those sentient beings, the Buddha divided these relics into pieces as small as mustard seeds. Ānanda!

When the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, he entered such a samādhi and divided these relics into pieces as small as mustard seeds.
However, the body of the Tathāgata does not experience pain; even when all his limbs and joints are dismembered and separated, he can cause the śarīra to remain like mustard seeds.

At that time, the Buddha, the Tathāgata, remains free from pain because he compassionately gathers and protects those sentient beings and future sentient beings, and causes them to attain peace and security in the various good realms.

“Regarding those who make offerings to the relics—honoring, welcoming, escorting, and reverently serving them with various adornments, various flowers, incense, perfumed ointments, powdered incense, robes, banners, flags, and many jeweled parasols, as well as song, dance, and music—I declare that they shall attain the fruit of Nirvāṇa, even unto the very limit of Nirvāṇa.”
“Ānanda! One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be a king named Aśoka in the city of Pāṭaliputra—one born of the Maurya clan—who will rule the world according to the Dharma.”

They shall come to have reverent faith in my Dharma; having attained such faith, they shall cause my relics to increase and spread widely, erecting eighty-four thousand stūpas for my relics in a single day and at a single moment.
Ānanda! Do not grieve; my relics shall be widely disseminated among devas and humans.
“Ānanda! [he said.]

"Setting aside for now the making of offerings to the Tathāgata in the present, and setting aside for now the making of offerings to my relics after my parinirvāṇa—even if they are as small as mustard seeds—Ānanda!

If there is one who, in a dream, sees a Buddha temple and gives rise to a mind of reverent faith, I declare that by this root of goodness that person shall attain nirvāṇa, attain the supreme nirvāṇa, and reach the very limit of nirvāṇa."
Ānanda! All the Buddhas who shall appear in the future world will, without exception, proclaim my meritorious conduct, just as I now praise the merits of the Buddhas of the past;
the future Buddhas proclaiming my name shall likewise be so.
“Ānanda! When I teach the Dharma, all those sentient beings who distance themselves from dust and leave behind defilement, thereby attaining the Dharma-eye—Ānanda!
All such sentient beings were previously matured by me when I was practicing the bodhisattva path.”
“Ānanda! If the merit from giving to the field of the Saṃgha is exhausted, and the merit from giving to the Saṃgha of the four directions is also exhausted;
yet the merit produced by giving to a Pratyekabuddha is not exhausted therein.”
If one performs meritorious deeds for the Buddha, they shall be inexhaustible.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
As I have previously stated, all meritorious deeds performed toward the various fields of merit shall result in the fruit of nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa."
Ānanda! Let alone those who have personally attended upon and made offerings to me; let alone those who will make offerings to my relics after my parinirvāṇa. Ānanda!

If there are those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and scatter even a single flower into the air, I perceive through my buddha-wisdom that their roots of goodness are immeasurable and inexpressible.

Ānanda! As for the roots of goodness cultivated by those sentient beings—those who, with a mind mindful of the Buddha, scattered even a single flower into the air—their wandering and transmigrating throughout this entire kalpa, from beginning to end, cannot be fully known.

During the period of saṃsāra, if one offers and scatters even a single flower before a Tathāgata, the resulting karmic fruit cannot be described; such a person may become a Brahmā King, a Śakra King, or a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning King. Because those roots of goodness are inexhaustible, they will certainly attain nirvāṇa and reach the ultimate limit of nirvāṇa.
Why is this so? Ānanda!

By offering a single flower to the great supernormal powers of such Buddhas, one obtains immeasurable rewards of merit, vast benefits, and a great mass of virtue that cannot be measured, is without limit, and will inevitably lead to the realm of Nirvāṇa.
“Ānanda! Those who perform meritorious deeds for the sake of the Buddha shall obtain such immeasurable and boundless rewards of merit;

even those who, regarding the Buddha, give rise to a single thought of resolve or a single moment of faith—I declare that such persons have perfected their holy life (*brahmacarya*), attained ultimate peace, and reached the very limit of the ultimate.”
Therefore, Ānanda!

If there are good men or good women who wish to attain sovereignty as lords of all the worlds—including the Brahmā kings, the wheel-turning sage-kings (cakravartin), the world-protecting four heavenly kings, the gods of the Thirty-three, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, and other various devas, as well as nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth—they should thus revere, welcome, honor, and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Whether one seeks the stage of a śrāvaka, the stage of a pratyekabuddha, or seeks unsurpassed *samyak-saṃbodhi*, such sons of good family and daughters of good family should likewise revere, honor, humble themselves before, and make offerings to them.

“Ānanda! In the past, when I was seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, at the abodes of immeasurable Buddhas, immeasurable hundreds of Buddhas, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, and even immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, I honored, revered, and humbled myself before them. I made offerings of robes, food and drink, seats, bedding, and medicinal decoctions required for the causes and conditions of illness. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, I offered those Buddhas various flower garlands, unguents, powdered incense, sandalwood, aloeswood, banners, flags, and precious canopies.”

After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they shall erect stūpas and shrines, adorning them in various ways, and with incense, flowers, unguents, powdered incense, song, dance, play, and hundreds of thousands of musical instruments, they shall reverently honor, respect, and humbly make offerings to them. This is for the sake of pitying all sentient beings in the world; for the benefit, peace, and happiness of devas and humans; so that those not yet delivered may be delivered; those not yet liberated may be liberated; those not yet at peace may find peace; and those not yet in nirvāṇa may attain nirvāṇa.

“Ānanda! When I scattered five stalks of *utpala* flowers upon the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I immediately realized the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Such roots of goodness are but a small portion of the resulting retribution.”

Ānanda! Do you wish to know the small portion of the merit and reward resulting from the five stalks of flowers I scattered before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṅkara, as well as my other roots of goodness?
Ānanda said: “So be it, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it.”
"So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata! Now is the very time;
we pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and reveal the fruit and retribution obtained from even a small root of goodness planted under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara."

At that time, the World-Honored One extended his golden right arm and released a single celestial utpala flower from one of his little fingers; its fragrance filled the trichiliocosm—the world-system of the Buddhas—and there was nowhere throughout the range of ten billion suns and moons where it did not pervade.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested this extraordinary and unprecedented phenomenon among the devas, humans, and asuras, in order to demonstrate that the blessings and rewards obtained from planting even a small root of goodness under the Buddhas are neither in vain nor diminished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas are inconceivable, And the Dharma of the Tathāgata is likewise so.
Those who can believe in what is inconceivable Will surely obtain inconceivable retribution."
Whether they possess perception or lack perception,
all sentient beings throughout immeasurable hundreds of billions of kalpas— should one make offerings to them all;
as well as all pratyekabuddhas and arhats free from outflows.
Throughout inconceivable eons, one might make offerings to all those Perfectly Awakened Ones,
whether they remain in the world or have entered parinirvāṇa;
yet even a single act of joining the palms in reverence brings forth merit far superior to that which precedes it.
The Buddha’s precepts are without flaw; he has attained mastery in samādhi;
he harbors no doubt regarding the Dharma; with the Buddha-eye, there is nothing he does not perceive.
