If one cultivates loving-kindness toward the Sugata for even a brief moment, whether by day or by night, [the merit is immeasurable].
The merit of such offerings is immeasurable; it is peerless and without compare within the three realms.
Throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas of the past, in the presence of the Guides of all worlds, he acted as a light among gods and humans, cultivating innumerable wholesome deeds.
While wandering through incalculable eons, the karmic rewards of that merit could never be exhausted;
by taking that merit as my causal condition, I was able to attain such supreme enlightenment.

In the past, out of compassion for sentient beings, I constantly performed supreme offerings at the abodes of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas in every lifetime; yet, the Buddhas did not grant me a prophecy of enlightenment.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, supreme among men, knew that my roots of goodness were not yet fully ripened;
though I practiced various virtues, I did not receive the prediction [of enlightenment], because I lacked such sublime patience.

I also saw that Dīpaṃkara Buddha; I offered five stalks of utpala flowers and spread my hair upon the mud so that the Buddha might tread upon it, whereupon I immediately realized the supreme dharma-patience of non-arising.
Then that Guide, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, immediately bestowed upon me a prophecy as I ascended into the air:
"In a future age, after incalculable eons (asaṃkhyeya), you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."
From the beginningless flow of birth and death, you have practiced immeasurable virtuous deeds;
out of compassion for sentient beings, you have endured all manner of suffering in pursuit of such supreme enlightenment.
Seeing the suffering of the world’s solitary and forlorn, I constantly practice giving out of a heart of compassion;
that merit is infinite and immeasurable, such that even a Guide could not fully describe it.
When I was practicing as a bodhisattva, I chanted the names of and made offerings to all the Sugatas,
the Heroes of the World, day and night for immeasurable billions of incalculable kalpas.

One, two, three, four, five up to ten; twenty, thirty—reciting these names in brief, he practiced out of compassion for all sentient beings, those whom the most supreme Buddhas had previously made offerings to.
When I originally practiced asceticism, I endured immeasurable sufferings;
throughout every lifetime, I did not abandon the bodhicitta, such that no Buddha could compare with me.
Throughout my wanderings through successive lifetimes, I have relinquished hundreds of thousands of millions of heads,
as well as jewels, kingdoms, and royal thrones, in order to seek the hearing of the Dharma and its many excellent expositions.
When I practiced for the sake of the unsurpassed True Dharma, with a profound mind I sought it with immeasurable zeal;
through generosity, ethical discipline, and patience, as well as diligence, I awakened to supreme Bodhi.
The power of all Buddhas is inconceivable, established through all their merits;
they are able to expound the inconceivable True Dharma and are also able to manifest supreme enlightenment.
Chapter Eleven: Planting Roots of Goodness. *The Sutra of Great Compassion*, Chapter Eleven: Planting Roots of Goodness. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda, saying:

"From the time I encountered Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I subsequently met another Buddha named Padmottara. For the sake of seeking anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I scattered golden lotuses as an offering to that Buddha."
Subsequently, I encountered a Buddha named Sarvalokāgrādhipati; I scattered silver flowers before that Buddha, seeking such omniscience as this.
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Paramocchraya-caryā (Extremely High Conduct); I offered him precious coins, seeking such inconceivable wisdom.
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Uttara-yaśas (Supreme Renown); I offered him various jewels, seeking such unobstructed wisdom.
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Śākyamuni; I scattered various flowers over that Buddha for the sake of seeking such unsurpassed bodhi.
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Tiṣya; I smeared and scattered red sandalwood powder over that Buddha, likewise for the sake of seeking unobstructed wisdom.
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Puṣya; with deep faith, for seven days and seven nights without blinking my eyes, I praised that World-Honored One with immeasurable verses.
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Vipaśyin, and I again scattered beans before that World-Honored One.
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Śikhin, and I offered a priceless precious robe to that Buddha.
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Viśvabhū, whom I honored with offerings of various delicacies and food. "Ānanda!
At the beginning of this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha who appeared named Krakucchanda; I practiced the pure life of brahmacarya under him for the sake of seeking such self-arisen wisdom."
Next, I encountered a Buddha named Kanakamuni, under whom I practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Following that, there was another Buddha named Kāśyapa, at whose time I likewise practiced the holy life.

At all these places where the Buddhas were, I sought Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; for my own deliverance and for the deliverance of those not yet delivered, for my own liberation and for the liberation of those not yet liberated, for my own attainment of nirvāṇa and for the attainment of nirvāṇa by those not yet attained to it.

Observe now how I have made offerings to so many immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas, World-Honored Ones—honoring, respecting, and reverently serving them—with the full possession of immeasurable virtuous merits, all for the sake of seeking this very Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Ānanda! You should know that through this sequence, even by planting a small root of goodness in the presence of the Buddha, one shall attain such great supernormal powers, great benefits, and vast merit.

“Ānanda! I have planted such inconceivable roots of merit for enlightenment under the Buddha; now I have obtained this inconceivable retribution—unequaled, unrivaled, and without limit—which you should believe.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"When I encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings, I was practicing the bodhisattva path;
I scattered five stalks of blue lotuses before that Buddha, and he immediately bestowed upon me the prediction of unsurpassed enlightenment."
Next there was a Buddha named Padmottara;
at that time I also encountered him and scattered golden jewel-flowers before that Buddha for the sake of seeking supreme enlightenment.
Next there was another Buddha, a Great Guide, named Sarvalokābhibhū.
I made offerings to those of supreme conduct and high renown—
Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni,
and Kāśyapa Buddha— all in order to seek the most sublime and excellent bodhi.
These and all other past Buddhas, I have honored with supreme offerings;
out of compassion for all sentient beings, I seek the unsurpassed, sublime Bodhi.
Having made offerings to those billions of Buddhas and fully accumulated roots of goodness,
he subdued the power of Māra and his retinue, and attained the path of sorrowless tranquility.
I have turned the unsurpassed Great Wheel of Dharma; for the sake of sentient beings, I have revealed the True Dharma.
To the devas, humans, nāgas, and kinnaras who were worthy vessels for Bodhi, my deliverance is complete.
I have already revealed the path of peace;
future Buddhas and their disciples, if they wish to deliver all who suffer, should cultivate my virtuous conduct.
The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Scroll Three;
The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: Entrusting the True Dharma through Various Parables At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:

"Setting aside for now the merits and benefits I have attained upon reaching bodhi, even the pratyekabuddhas did not possess the merits and benefits I had while originally practicing the bodhisattva path, let alone the śrāvakas and other sentient beings."

Ānanda! When I was a bodhisattva, I practiced asceticism for a long time; I renounced my royal throne, my children, my wife, and all my court ladies; I gave up my life, my hands, feet, head, eyes, ears, nose, flesh, blood, marrow, and underwent all manner of immeasurable suffering—all of this was solely for the sake of you all, out of my longing for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Ānanda! All things difficult to relinquish I have already relinquished; all the manifold sufferings I have undergone were for the sake of sentient beings. Ānanda!
If I were to describe these merits in detail, they would be inexhaustible;
those who hear them would become bewildered and distressed, let alone those who speak of them. "Ānanda!

If there are sentient beings who give rise to even a single thought of compassion for the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, for his past cultivation of the bodhisattva’s ascetic practices, and speak these words:
"For our sake, you have fully endured immeasurable and various kinds of pain and difficult tasks."
"Ānanda! I say that even those who have given rise to the thought of awakening once will certainly attain final nirvāṇa; how much more so for those who have planted roots of goodness under me?"

Ānanda! There may be foolish people who are obstinate and lacking in faith; having heard that I originally practiced the ascetic austerities of a bodhisattva without giving rise to even a single thought of compassion, and hearing that the Tathāgata does not speak of great benefit, nor do they respect or believe that all these supreme practices can lead to nirvāṇa.
Ānanda! Such meritorious benefits and supreme dharmas as these do not exist even among the pratyekabuddhas, let alone among all śrāvakas or ordinary worldlings.
“Ānanda! The great compassion attained by those who practice the path of a bodhisattva is not something that can be possessed by pratyekabuddhas. Ānanda!”

If there are those who practice the bodhisattva path as I do and attain great compassion, having attained great compassion, they shall all surely attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; therefore, this Dharma is encompassed by great kindness and great compassion.
For these reasons, these qualities are absent in the Pratyekabuddhas;
for this reason, they cannot become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, nor do they possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great loving-kindness, or great compassion.

“Ānanda! I remember that in the past, while practicing the bodhisattva path and seeking the sublime Dharma, my mind was constantly filled with alarm and dread regarding birth and death. As I cultivated great compassion for all sentient beings, I saw in a dream that the Great Iron Ring Mountains were crumbling and collapsing. In the midst of the world-systems, there were beings in the great hells who were being tormented by the hell-wardens; their bodies were shattered and completely ablaze like masses of fire, undergoing intense suffering as agonizing as the loss of life itself.”
I went to where they were, and those sentient beings joined their palms in prostration and spoke these words:
"O Benevolent One!
May you now enjoy happiness;”
We now endure the sufferings of hell, which are so agonizing and unbearable that they are like the pain of losing one's life; we have no rescue, no protection, no refuge, and no resort.
"O Great Man!
If you wish to rescue me from such suffering as this, you are certainly capable of doing so. Ānanda!
At that time, I gave rise to great compassion for those sentient beings in hell, and immediately within my dream, I wept with tears flowing like the waters of the Ganges River.
I then comforted those beings, saying: "O noble ones!
"Do not give rise to fear; I shall cause you all to be liberated from this mass of suffering. Ānanda!
At that time, I gathered those sentient beings in the hells together in one place, rubbed the crowns of their heads with my right hand, and addressed them, saying:
"O virtuous ones!
Do not give way to fear; I shall certainly deliver you all.
Having spoken these words, the masses of fire in the hells were immediately extinguished, and those sentient beings attained peace and happiness in that very instant.
"Ānanda! At that time, having awakened from my dream, I shook out my robe, took up my tears, and placed them in a vessel. Ānanda!"
I originally cultivated the bodhisattva practices while fully possessing this dharma of great compassion; how much more so now that I have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Ānanda!
"You should know that such a Dharma as this is not even within the capacity of a pratyekabuddha, let alone a śrāvaka or an ordinary person,
Ānanda!"
If one possesses this Dharma, that person is practicing the bodhisattva path. "Ānanda!
You should observe that when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he possessed such a heart of compassion, benefit, and great pity toward all sentient beings."
If I were to proclaim these merits in full through the activity of speech, I would not reach their limit. "Ānanda!
In a past age, there was a great merchant leader who, for the sake of gathering treasures, led a company of merchants into the great ocean."
The ship they were traveling in was filled with all kinds of precious treasures, but when it reached the middle of the ocean, the vessel suddenly broke apart.
At that time, the merchants were seized by fear and fell into extreme distress; among them, some caught hold of planks, some floated on the water, and some lost their lives.
Ānanda! At that time, I was the leader of those merchants, and by means of a life-raft, I crossed the great ocean in safety.
Then there were five men who called out to the leader of the merchants, saying:
“O Great Being, Merchant Leader!
We pray only that you grant us fearlessness.
Having spoken these words, the merchant leader then addressed them, saying:
"O noble men! Do not give way to fear;
I shall enable you all to cross this great ocean safely. Thus [spoke the Buddha], Ānanda!
At that time, the merchant leader, girded with a sharp sword, thought to himself:
"The nature of the great ocean is such that it does not harbor corpses; if I now sacrifice my own life, these merchants will surely be able to cross the perils of the great sea."

Having formed this thought, he immediately called the merchants and placed them upon his body, instructing them to hold on firmly; among those merchants, some rode upon his back, some embraced his shoulders, and some grasped his thighs.

At that time, desiring to bestow fearlessness upon them, the merchant leader cultivated a mind of great compassion, gave rise to great valor, and exerted the power of his body and mind; he then severed the life-faculty with a sharp sword and quickly brought about his own death.
Then the great ocean cast up their corpses onto the shore; at that time, the five merchants were able to cross the sea in safety and peace, returning to Jambudvīpa without mishap or difficulty.
Ānanda! Could that caravan leader at that time have been anyone else?
It was I myself.
The five merchants are these five bhikṣus of today.

Just as those five bhikṣus were formerly delivered across the great ocean, they have now likewise been delivered across this great ocean of birth and death, and established upon the fearless shore of nirvāṇa.
“Ānanda! You should now observe what ascetic practices you have fulfilled.
How have you attained immeasurable merit to become a bodhisattva-mahāsattva?”
Ānanda! These merits should be understood in their proper sequence; they are not even attainable by pratyekabuddhas. Ānanda!
Just as the merits of the bodhisattvas are thus, because pratyekabuddhas lack these qualities, they do not become Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, nor do they attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Ānanda! It is by being able to practice such ascetic austerities that one becomes a bodhisattva who possesses great compassion and feels pity for all sentient beings. Ānanda!"

Furthermore, there are foolish people who do not give rise to respectful faith toward me, the Buddha; because of these causes and conditions, they cannot produce the fundamental seeds for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor can they realize unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*.
If they were to give rise to respectful faith in my mind, they would immediately be able to produce the seeds of *bodhi* and would be able to realize *nirvāṇa*.
"Ānanda! By practicing the limited portion of the path, one attains a limited portion of merit; by practicing the complete portion of the path, one attains the complete portion of merit. Ānanda!"
I shall further explain other practices that lead to certainty.

If there are sentient beings who can even give rise to a single thought of reverent faith, they will take this root of goodness as a seed; how much more so for those who plant superior roots of goodness?

Ānanda! If there are those who plant roots of goodness with the Buddha, even if they bring to mind the Buddha for but a single thought-moment, I declare that they are like nectar, the ultimate nectar.

“Ānanda! A practitioner should recollect the Tathāgata in every way; that is to say, they should recollect what the Tathāgata has recollected, recollect the Tathāgata’s roots of goodness, and recollect the lineage of the Tathāgata.”
His lineage is not of common origin, as he is born of the noble Ikṣvāku clan;
his name is "Sun" (Sūrya), for he acts as a light to dispel all darkness. Ānanda!
“Ānanda! Because I was born into the Śākya clan, my lineage is pure.”

One should contemplate the Tathāgata’s birth; contemplate the Tathāgata’s lineage; contemplate the Tathāgata’s clan; contemplate the Tathāgata’s perfection of accumulated wealth; contemplate the Tathāgata’s physical beauty; contemplate the Tathāgata’s land of birth; contemplate the Tathāgata’s marks; contemplate the Tathāgata’s secondary characteristics; contemplate the Tathāgata’s ten powers; contemplate the Tathāgata’s four fearlessnesses; contemplate the Tathāgata’s eighteen unique qualities; contemplate the Tathāgata’s perfection of birth; contemplate the Tathāgata’s excellence; contemplate the Tathāgata’s freedom from delusion; contemplate the Tathāgata’s perfection of past conduct; contemplate the Tathāgata’s perfection of vows; contemplate the Tathāgata’s perfection of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; contemplate the Tathāgata’s perfection of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; and contemplate the Tathāgata’s perfection of dignified deportment.

Ānanda! If there are people who, according to how they recollect the Buddha, obtain great supernormal powers, great benefits, and vast merit from each of those respective qualities—these are like ambrosia, the foremost ambrosia, and the ultimate ambrosia.

“Ānanda! When I was practicing the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) as a bodhisattva in the past, even when I observed its merit with my Buddha-wisdom, I could not find its limit; how much less so for the other merits such as the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā), the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā), the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), the perfection of meditation (dhyānapāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā)?”

If even the Buddha’s wisdom, when examining all the merits of those bodhisattvas who have not yet received their prediction, cannot find their limit, how much less so for the merits of those who have received their prediction?
How much more so, then, regarding all the merits attained at the time of becoming a Buddha?
Even if one were to observe and proclaim them for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, one could never reach their limit.
Why is this? Because the merits of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha are immeasurable, Ānanda!
I speak thus because I observe this benefit with my wisdom of reality.
If anyone recollects the merits and benefits of me, the Bodhisattva, and gives rise to a heart of reverence and faith, they shall all, by virtue of these roots of goodness, attain final nirvana.
Therefore, Ānanda, do not grieve or lament.

For the sake of bringing great benefit and great protection to you and all the devas and humans, I have already taught the Dharma, enabling them to proceed toward the unsurpassed peace and security of final Nirvāṇa.
"You should all diligently cultivate skillful means in this matter; be careful not to be negligent.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"In the latter part of this night, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. This is your final opportunity to see me, your final reception of my transformation, and your final assembly with me."
From this day forward, you shall no longer see me, and I likewise shall no longer see you.
Cease, O bhikṣus! Do not grieve or lament.
"All things beloved and all objects that accord with one's wishes must inevitably disperse.

O Bhikṣus! As for phenomena that are subject to birth, phenomena that exist, conditioned phenomena, differentiated phenomena, cognizable phenomena, and phenomena produced by causes and conditions that are destined to decay—if they were not to perish, such a thing could never be."
"O bhikṣus!
Even if one were to remain for a long time, one must eventually depart.
O bhikṣus!"
All who are born must die; all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without permanence or stability, and are ultimately subject to change. Monks!
Birth and death are suffering; Nirvana is bliss.
If you wish to cause those who have not attained to attain, those who have not reached to reach, and those who have not realized to realize, you should seek this with diligence.
O bhikṣus! Diligently cultivate skillful means; be careful not to be negligent.
Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, were heedful, they attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as well as all other wholesome dharmas that assist the path.
Therefore, you should receive my transformation.

At that time, the great assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, and others—having heard these final instructions, were filled with grief and distress. Pierced by the arrows of sorrow, they wept and shed tears, wailing most bitterly, and spoke thus: "Bhagavān!
How swiftly has he entered parinirvāṇa? Sugata!
How swiftly has he entered parinirvāṇa?
"The Eye of the World has perished; the world is plunged into blindness and darkness—how sudden this is!
How can I now be so swiftly separated from the Jewel of sentient beings?

At that time, having heard these words, Ānanda gazed up at the Tathāgata with unblinking eyes. He then fell into deep reflection, wailing and weeping piteously, throwing his body to the ground like a great tree felled by an axe and falling down a steep precipice.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Cease, do not grieve or lament.
Did I not previously speak to you in this way?"
"All things that are pleasing to the mind and all beloved objects must inevitably be separated from.

That which is subject to birth, subject to existence, conditioned, differentiated, and cognizable—being a phenomenon produced by causes and conditions that is subject to decay and destruction—it is impossible for it not to cease."
Having heard these words, the Venerable Ānanda immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Bhagavān! How could I not be distressed?”
Sugata! How could I not be grieved?

I am about to be separated from such a jewel among sentient beings, a vehicle for all beings, a guide for sentient beings, one sought by the world, the refuge of the world, and the Great Teacher of gods and humans.
Therefore, Blessed One! How could I not be sorrowful? Sugata!
"How could I not be grieved, World-Honored One?

I shall be separated from one who is a great compassionate friend to all sentient beings in the world, a jewel that is the eye of the entire world, and a maker of light; yet I marvel at myself that my heart does not shatter into a hundred pieces."
"World-Honored One!
I am further struck with wonder that I remain here without having met my death.
World-Honored One!"
Furthermore, I was astonished that my body had not been shattered, remaining as solid as a grain of wheat.
World-Honored One!
I then reflected further:
"That we have now attained such a state as not to die is entirely due to the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power.
Blessed One! How could I not be filled with sorrow?"
O Sugata! How could I not be sorrowful?
Now that this One Who Rides the Vehicle Common to All Beings, the Teacher of the World, the Compassionate One for the World, shall not remain tomorrow and can no longer be seen.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Do you love me? Ānanda replied:
“It is most wonderful, Blessed One!
It is most wonderful, Sugata!
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! How do you love me? Ānanda replied:
“I love the Blessed One; this love cannot be exhausted by verbal expressions through the karma of speech, nor can it be fully expressed by means of analogies.
Bhagavān, my love is such as this.”
Sugata! I love it thus.
World-Honored One!
"Bhagavān, I would not begrudge even my own body and life for the sake of the Tathāgata;
such is my love."
"Sugata, I love it thus.
World-Honored One!"
"Bhagavān, my love for the Tathāgata is such that only the Buddha himself can bear witness to it;
Bhagavān, my love is indeed thus."
"Sugata! I love it thus.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
“If you love me, extend your right hand and come forward.
At that time, Ānanda immediately extended his right hand.
Then the World-Honored One took Ānanda’s hand with his own golden right hand—its palm soft and its color like purple mineral—and spoke these words:
"Ānanda! If you love me, you should perform for me that which is the act of loving.
What is the act of loving that I have performed?"

I entrust to you this great Dharma-treasury of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, which I have cultivated over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas. You should comply with it; as I have turned it, so shall you turn it, causing it to be widely practiced without interruption, and do not become one who causes the Dharma to perish midway.
Ānanda! I shall now provide you with protection so that the True Dharma and Vinaya spoken by the Buddha may increase, neither declining nor being lost or destroyed.
"I shall now speak a parable, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through parables.

Suppose there were a noble and wealthy elder, possessing great riches and abundant wealth, with many storehouses and lacking nothing that might be required; such treasures and jewels he shared not with others.
He was endowed with a distinguished lineage, his ancestry being profound and remote, and all the causal conditions of his birth were likewise complete."
In this way, the householder raised a son.
Once the son had grown up, he diligently instructed him in arithmetic, writing, seals, and various other profound and subtle crafts and profound wisdoms.
Once the son had completed his studies, at a later time the elder said to him:
"I have now finished what was to be done for you; since you have mastered calculation, writing, seals, profound craftsmanship, and profound wisdom, today is my final instruction."

"All wealth and treasures are my possession; I now entrust them all to you. From this day forward, you should train in three matters so that you may preserve my family lineage and its ancient legacy."
"What are the three?
First, desire; second, diligence; third, heedfulness.
In this way, the noble, wealthy, and affluent elder skillfully instructed his only son, yet that son was deluded and negligent, exhausting all the father’s and mother’s property and wealth.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Did that son of the householder receive his father’s instruction?
Ānanda said: “No, Blessed One! No, Sugata!”
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! Would such an elder be performing the duties of a father toward his son?”
Ānanda said: “I shall do so, Blessed One! I shall do so, Sugata!”
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! The Tathāgata is the father of the world, and you are like his only son."
"Today is my final instruction; I entrust to you this treasury of the unsurpassed Dharma-jewel, which I have practiced for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas."
You all should also train yourselves in three matters. What are these three?
First, aspiration; second, diligence; third, heedfulness.

In this way, if you abide in these three matters, this treasury of the unsurpassed Dharma-jewel, which I have practiced for incalculable eons, will endure for a long time; those who have not yet attained mastery of the wholesome dharmas will attain it, and those who have already attained it will not fall away from it.

Therefore, you all should firmly uphold this treasury of the Dharma-jewel of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have practiced for incalculable kalpas: cause those who have not yet established themselves in the three matters to establish themselves in them; cause those who have not yet attained mastery of the wholesome dharmas to attain such mastery; and cause those who have already attained mastery not to fall away from it.
Why is this? It is because I act out of compassion and pity for the sake of benefiting all the world, and in order to bring them peace and happiness. Ānanda!
"I have already fulfilled my duties as a father and as a kinsman toward the world;
I have done for you all that was to be done. Furthermore, Ānanda!"
The Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that I have practiced throughout incalculable kalpas shall, due to three causes and conditions, come to be obscured.
What are these three?
First, lack of faith; second, not abiding in resolute practice; third, failure to repent.

Therefore, Ānanda, you should now protect and uphold the precious treasury of the True Dharma by establishing deep faith, practicing resolute repentance, and applying the three skillful means of aspiration, diligence, and heedfulness.
Thus, you have done what ought to be done as a son toward me, the Honored One of the Dharma and Father of the World.
Ānanda, for this reason,
I shall speak another parable so that this unsurpassed treasure-store of the True Dharma may be successfully accomplished and entrusted with even greater care.

By means of this analogy, those who possess wisdom, upon hearing this teaching, attain understanding; they further develop an even deeper, superior love, respect, and faith, and then give rise to this thought:

"For our sake, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni, at the time of his parinirvāṇa, took Ānanda’s hand with his own right hand and entrusted to him this Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which he had practiced for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas."
“It is, for example, like a caravan leader who has traveled a long distance on the road and has already completed all that was to be done.
Ānanda, what do you think?”
"Will that merchant leader return home,
or will he remain on the road? Ānanda said:
“World-Honored One!
He has returned home and is no longer staying on the road.
“Ānanda! [the Buddha replied.]

Thus, the Tathāgata—the father of the world, the kinsman of the world, the guide of the world—is a great caravan leader who, by means of the wisdom of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, has already completed all that was to be done; there remains no further Buddha-work to be performed. All sentient beings who were to be delivered have been delivered, and those who were to be delivered have been well-disciplined.
“Ānanda! There are three things that, being unfulfilled and unattained, prevent the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha from passing into parinirvāṇa.
What are these three?
It refers to a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet attained the stage of non-retrogression.

If, during a time when the unsurpassed true Dharma of the Tathāgata has vanished—whether after one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, a hundred thousand kalpas, or even a hundred thousand koṭi-nayuta kalpas—they have not yet been able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, then although the time for the parinirvāṇa of those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, has arrived, [the Buddhas] perceive that this bodhisattva’s roots of goodness are not yet matured. In order to bring them to maturity and cause them to abide in non-retrogression, they employ their supernormal powers to empower the bodhisattva’s own person so that they remain in the world without passing away.

Once this bodhisattva has attained the stage of non-retrogression, the Buddha-Tathāgata immediately bestows upon him the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as his successor in the sequential order of succession; only then does that Buddha-Tathāgata enter into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

Therefore, I now bestow upon Maitreya and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas the prediction of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, causing them to abide in the state of avaivartika; this is that which all buddhas, out of compassion for sentient beings, ought to do and have already done.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If there are sentient beings who ought to attain liberation through the Tathāgata but have not yet been delivered, the Tathāgata will never enter parinirvāṇa."

If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows that for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas no other Buddha has appeared in the world—whether in his own world or in other worlds—and that among all sentient beings within the five realms of existence, whether after one year, a hundred years, a thousand years, a hundred thousand years, or a hundred thousand billion nayutas of years, even up to one kalpa or more than one kalpa, these beings are ones who should be liberated by me, and not by any of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

Having known this through his Buddha-wisdom, although the time for that Buddha, the World-Honored One, to enter parinirvāṇa had arrived, out of compassion for them, he empowered his own person with supernormal powers to remain in the world without passing away, until they had reached maturity and were subsequently liberated.
"Ānanda! This is the second [task] that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, must perform; having performed it, they then enter parinirvāṇa without remainder.
Furthermore, Ānanda!"

The profound meanings contained within all that the Tathāgata has spoken—whether in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Mātṛkā—cannot be understood through collective deliberation by the great assembly of Śrāvakas, whether they be those still in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Within that assembly, should there be a bhikṣu who conceives a doubt and wishes to inquire, yet out of reverence for the Buddha, fears causing disturbance, and does not dare to ask immediately;
then the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knowing this through his buddha-wisdom, manifests a bhikṣu and approaches the Tathāgata, asking:
"World-Honored One!..."
"How should this task be performed?
The Buddha then addressed that manifested bhikṣu, saying: "Bhikṣu!"
"This task must be performed in this manner.
Ānanda! These are the three tasks that all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, must necessarily perform; until these matters are fulfilled, they do not enter parinirvāṇa.
“All these things I have now accomplished and fulfilled; there is nothing further to be done, and nothing further to be said. Ānanda!

I have now taught the training in the Vinaya and the Prātimokṣa for the sake of my disciples; for the sake of ending suffering, I have shown the true path and taught the practice that leads to certainty, so that they may perform their task.”
Therefore, Ānanda!
From this day forward, you must be careful not to speak what I have not spoken, and do not allow what I have spoken to be interrupted. Ānanda!
As I have taught, you should train yourselves in this way and act accordingly; be careful not to indulge in negligence.
Because of non-negligence, you shall attain the fruits of the Path.
For this reason, I command you all: do not grieve, do not lament.

“Ānanda! This very night, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. I shall now relinquish my own land and my own realm; I shall never again return to this world, nor shall I go to other worlds—other worlds being the places of rebirth in future lives.”
From this day forward, you shall no longer see me, and I shall no longer see you. Ānanda!

I am about to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*—a nirvāṇa that is tranquil and cool, free from dust and devoid of defilement, wherein all suffering ceases; having abandoned the cave-dwelling of the body, it is without birth, aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, or anything disagreeable; it is free from all regrets, the meeting with the hated, and separation from the beloved. Just as the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, along with all their śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, have already departed, are now departing, or will depart.
“Ānanda! You should now observe that even I still cherish that nirvana without remainder.

Yet there are foolish ordinary people who do not cherish that supreme, wondrous, tranquil, and blissful nirvana, nor are they able to give rise to a single thought of resolve to accord with liberation.”
If such a person can give rise to the thought of enlightenment for even a single moment, by this causal condition they shall take it as a seed and attain nirvana.
Ānanda! How could all ordinary worldlings possess such power?
"All ordinary worldlings are weak and powerless, Ānanda!
In my observation, all foolish ordinary worldlings are like parched barley."
Therefore, Ānanda!
How could foolish worldlings possess power?
How could they possess peace?

"Ānanda! All those who are unable to give rise to the thought of enlightenment and accord with liberation in a single moment—if they can give rise to that thought, they will certainly obtain the seeds of nirvāṇa."
All foolish ordinary people lack the power of ethical discipline, the power of meditative concentration, and the power of wisdom. Ānanda!

I have fully perfected the immeasurable powers of a Buddha; I am endowed with the powers of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—each numbering incalculable, inconceivable, immeasurable, and peerless—as well as the power of shame, the power of remorse, the power of long-term accumulation, the power of knowledge, the power of equanimity, the power of merit, the power of wisdom, the power of the faculties, the power of empowerment, and the ten powers. Yet, even so, I still cherish that nirvāṇa without remainder.

“Ānanda! There are ordinary beings who are dull-witted and devoid of wisdom, possessing little knowledge of the Dharma, and who take pleasure in being bound by the shackles of the prison of birth and death; they are unable even for a single thought-moment to resolve their minds toward liberation. You should cause them to obtain the fundamental seeds of nirvāṇa.”
Ānanda! Thus, the various sūtras praised and spoken by the Tathāgata shall remain for the sake of the future.

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, there are those in the future age who hear them, and having heard them, they give rise to the resolve, they will immediately enter the treasure-trove of the True Dharma, the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
“Ānanda! I shall speak a parable so that you may gain a superior and profound understanding of its meaning. Ānanda!”
It is like a caravan leader who, leading a multitude of merchants across a vast and perilous wilderness, brings them safely to the City of Fearlessness, free from the dangers of bandits.

Among them, one person loses his companions and falls behind; overcome with extreme terror, he follows their tracks and pursues the merchants, enduring great suffering until he finally crosses the dangerous path and rejoins his fellow travelers.
Ānanda! Thus it is that, having attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, the Tathāgata has expounded such sūtras as these to remain for the sake of the future.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there are good sons and good daughters who hear this teaching;
having heard it, they resolve their minds and come to the citadel of the true Dharma treasure that I have left behind—the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Having reached the city of the true Dharma, they shall contemplate and recollect it, protect and uphold it, and proclaim my treasury of Dharma treasures.

Ānanda! For the sake of even a single person, I would entrust this unsurpassed, true Dharma to you so that you may uphold it firmly; how much more so for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings?

Therefore, I now entrust to you this treasure-house of the true Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which I have practiced for billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas. You should recite it well and uphold it firmly, explaining and analyzing it for the fourfold assembly of pure faith, and do not become one who causes the extinction of the Dharma in the interim.
“Ānanda! In future ages, there will be sentient beings who, not having heard the meaning of such sūtras, will fall into despondency and retreat. Therefore, Ānanda!”
I shall now provide an analogy.

Suppose there were a noble, wealthy, and eminent householder who possessed abundant riches and treasures, whose storehouses were overflowing, and who had everything necessary for life fully provided; yet that householder had only one son who had traveled far away to another land.
At that time, the elder fell gravely ill, and his suffering was extreme.
As his life drew to a close, he entrusted many precious objects—*maṇi* jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, and gold, silver, and coinage—to another elder, saying:
"You should know this: my son has already traveled far away to another land, yet I am now afflicted by a grave illness and shall soon pass away."
"For the sake of my son, I entrust these immeasurable storehouses of wealth and treasures to you.

When my son returns from another region, instruct him on my behalf so that he does not become negligent; ensure that he remains firmly established in the dharma of non-negligence, and only then deliver these storehouses and treasures to him."
When handing over the treasure, one should say these words:
"Young man!
When your father was on the verge of death in the past, he entrusted this treasure to me for your sake."
I now return this to you; it is your own property which you should accept. Be careful not to be negligent; maintain and guard it firmly so that it does not come to ruin.
When that noble and wealthy elder had spoken these words, he immediately entrusted his many precious possessions to him, and the other elder accepted them.
Not long after he had accepted it, the son of that elder returned from another region, yet the other elder did not return any of the entrusted goods to him. Ānanda!
"What do you think?
Whose fault is this?
The Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
It is the fault of the trustee, not that of any other person. Why is this so?”
"Because the person who received the deposit personally accepted those many precious objects from that wealthy and noble elder, yet did not return them to the son.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
The wealthy and noble elder represents the Tathāgata;
one whose life is ending represents the Tathāgata’s desire to enter parinirvāṇa;
and the "only son" represents the sons and daughters of good family who possess pure faith in future ages.
Those who travel to distant lands are a metaphor for the transmigration through the five destinies;
the great treasure store is a metaphor for the unsurpassed great Dharma-treasure store cultivated by the Tathāgata over billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas;
and the elder to whom the treasure is entrusted is a metaphor for you all—the great śrāvakas, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and protectors of the true Dharma.

Ānanda! This unsurpassed great Dharma-treasury, which has been cultivated over the course of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, is entrusted by me to you, as well as to Mahākāśyapa, Maitreya, and other great bodhisattvas, for the sake of all good sons and good daughters in future ages.
If you are able to follow my entrustment, then to all those sons of the Buddha who are to be transformed and possess pure faith in future ages, you should bestow upon them the treasure of the Dharma.
Why is this? Ānanda!
There are sentient beings who were matured by me in the past when I was a bodhisattva, yet because of their evil karma, they have fallen into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts.

In this way, after the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, these sentient beings will escape the evil realms and be born among human beings. As their faculties grow and reach maturity, they will be able to give rise to reverent faith within my Dharma through even slight causes and conditions. Among them, some may choose to leave the household life; upon hearing the various sūtras I have taught, they shall initiate superior practices and attain parinirvāṇa, whether by means of the Śrāvaka Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, or the Mahāyāna.

“Ānanda! For the sake of future good sons and good daughters, I entrust to you this unsurpassed great Dharma-treasury, which I have practiced for hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, so that they may hear it.”
Why is this? If those sentient beings do not hear this true path and sublime Dharma, they will surely fall away.
Therefore, for the sake of those sons of good family in the future, I now entrust this great treasury of the Dharma to you; if they hear it, they shall have no further decline.
"For this reason, I shall again provide a parable. Ānanda!
It is as if a wheel-turning monarch were to open wide his treasuries and command his officials in charge:
"O noble sons!

You should practice generosity toward all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, beggars, and travelers. According to their needs, give food to those seeking food, drink to those needing drink, and vehicles to those requiring vehicles; furthermore, provide flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, clothing, bedding, pure dwellings, and the necessities for sustaining life."
"Having received the king's command, the various treasury officials did not carry out the distribution.
Ānanda, what do you think?"
"Whose fault is this?
Ānanda replied,
"O Great Virtuous Blessed One!"
"These were the faults of the ministers of the treasury, not of the Wheel-Turning King.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
It is so, it is so. As the Dharma King, throughout billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have extensively gathered such a great treasury of the Dharma.

Having attained self-awakening, I desire to cause it to increase and expand; I shall reveal and proclaim it among devas and humans, even for you to reveal, and for all those who revere and believe—śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and all ordinary people seeking the meaning of the Dharma—so that they may all hear it.
Therefore, Ānanda, I now entrust to you this great treasury of the Dharma—

which I have already extensively revealed— lest there be fault in me, the Tathāgata, if you do not widely proclaim and analyze it for the sake of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, householders, and all ordinary persons who delight in the meaning of the Dharma, and who possess pure faith.
Why is this so? Ānanda!

I am the Unsurpassed Dharma-Cakravartin King; I possess vast treasuries of the merit of the Dharma-jewels, abundant wealth of the seven factors of enlightenment that aid the path, and am fully endowed with the ten powers and fearlessnesses. Having attained sovereign mastery over all dharmas, I am therefore called the Dharma King.

"You shall uphold these eighty-four thousand treasuries of the True Dharma of mine and expound them fully for the sake of those who seek the meaning of the Dharma—be they śramaṇas, brahmins, elders, householders, faithful ordinary persons, or Dharma masters—without giving rise to discrimination, and do not become one who causes the extinction of the Dharma midway."
Therefore, Ānanda!

If you can expound and reveal to the fourfold assembly this unsurpassed Dharma-treasure of the Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi which I have practiced for hundreds of millions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, then you will be free from all faults before the Tathāgata;
if you do not speak it, there will be great transgression.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

If a bhikṣu who is an arhat with outflows exhausted, because he has realized the unconditioned, is unable to analyze and explain it for others, such a person does not benefit the Tathāgata, the Teacher, nor does he protect and uphold my True Dharma."
Therefore, I now entrust this Dharma to you.
Why is this? Ānanda!
It is, for example, as if there were a person who, carrying a grass torch, returned home from a great darkness, while many others also wished to cross through that darkness.
That person holding the torch was able to rely on this grass torch to cross the darkness and reach his own home; having arrived, he extinguished it and did not give it to the others.
Ānanda! What do you think?

Since this person knows that the grass torch has not yet burned out, and knows that the great assembly all wish to cross over the darkness, yet uses the torch for himself and does not give it to others—can this be called right action, or is it not good?
Ānanda said: “No, Blessed One! No, Sugata!”
The Buddha said, "So it is,
so it is, Ānanda!"

If there is a bhikṣu who has attained the fruit of arhatship and realized the unconditioned dharma, yet, although he knows that the great assembly is crossing over the darkness of birth and death, does not analyze and explain for others the jewel of the Dharma practiced by me over incalculable kalpas so that it may increase and expand—such a person is not called a teacher who benefits others, nor is he called one who upholds my true Dharma.
Therefore, Ānanda!

I now entrust to you this Dharma-treasure, which I have practiced for billions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, so that you may uphold it firmly and expound it extensively for others, ensuring that such a true path is not severed, and that you do not become one who causes the Dharma to perish at the end.

“Ānanda! If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who, having themselves established themselves in this Dharma-treasure, are able to analyze and explain it for others—this Dharma-treasure which I have practiced for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas—you should entrust it to them and give them their share.”
Therefore, Ānanda!

This second entrustment of the wholesome dharmas practiced by me over these hundreds of millions of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas is for the sake of all sentient beings in the future; do not allow such sentient beings to fail to hear them and thereby suffer loss and decline.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!

It is like a noble, wealthy, and eminent householder who possesses many storehouses, fully supplied with everything necessary for life, such as mani-jewels, pearls, coral, conch shells, and other treasures."
At that time, an enemy burned his storehouse.

Furthermore, this householder had various enemies and hostile friends who constantly took pleasure in doing him harm; some did not wish for him to obtain joy, and others did not wish for him to attain peace and security.
When those enemies saw that great fire burning the storehouse, they abandoned it and stood there in silence, not extinguishing the fire.

Furthermore, that householder had other kinsmen and friends who were always compassionate and intent on his welfare, desiring to bring him peace and security; yet upon seeing the fire, they too abandoned it and stood in silence, unwilling to extinguish it.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Can such a friend be said to have correctly set out in accordance with the principle?
Ānanda said: “No, Blessed One! No, Sugata!”
The Buddha said: "Ānanda!

Would those friends, seeing that great fire burning their storehouse, abandon it and fail to rescue it, such that the fire would instead increase in intensity and burn the entire storehouse to ashes?"
Ānanda said: “So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!”
The Buddha said, “So it is,
so it is, Ānanda!”

When the Dharma-treasure of the unsurpassed roots of goodness cultivated by me over billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas is being destroyed, there will be bhikṣus who lack reverence and faith, who violate the pure precepts, and who practice evil dharmas; they will act as leaders in places of song and dance, take no pleasure in renouncing desire or practicing meditative concentration, have minds that are largely distracted, and be indolent and lazy; they will hear little of the Dharma and take no delight in reading or reciting it.
"How can one analyze and explain it for others, enabling them to hear and uphold the Dharma-treasure?
"Furthermore, Ānanda! It is like this:
suppose there is a consecrated Kṣatriya great king who has only one son, who has traveled far away and is not present."
When that Kṣatriya king was afflicted by a grave illness, having fallen ill, he took various treasures and diverse goods and went to entrust them to his ministers and elders, saying:
"If my son returns, you should establish him to succeed to the royal throne and hand over all these storehouses to him."
The ministers and elders each separately received what was entrusted to them by that king; once they had accepted the entrustment, the king passed away.
After the king’s death, his son returned from his travels and immediately succeeded to the royal throne.
Once he had ascended the throne and attained full sovereignty, the ministers and elders did not return those treasures and wealth to him, saying:
"Excellent, Great King!"
"Ruling according to the True Dharma, he has bestowed these precious objects upon us. Ānanda,
what do you think?
“Are the ministers and householders to whom he entrusted [the kingdom] at fault for that king?
Ānanda replied, “It is so, Blessed One.”
"So it is, Sugata! That indeed is a fault.
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! Those traveling far away are a metaphor for sentient beings in the five realms of existence;
the sick person is a metaphor for the Buddha’s desire to enter nirvana.”
The "Great Treasure Store" is a metaphor for the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
the "ministers and elders" are metaphors for the various arhats;

and "entrusting the precious objects" is a metaphor for my entrusting to you this Dharma-treasure, which I have practiced for billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya kalpas, and so forth, for the sake of those future disciples.

“Ānanda! In future ages there will be sentient beings—those whom I have matured in the past—who, due to their evil karma, were born in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts. After my parinirvāṇa, they will die there and be reborn among humans; their faculties will grow and reach maturity, and within my Dharma they will give rise to reverent faith. Some will leave the household life, some will remain as householders, some will attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, and even some will attain the stage of *arhat*. Some will pass away while still on the path of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), some will develop deep faith in the stage of a Buddha, and some will plant the various roots of goodness for human and celestial realms. In this way, they shall fully obtain benefit.”
Those who have attained such reverent faith speak thus:
"The Father of the World has entrusted us well, and we have further attained superior reverent faith."
"Ānanda! For their sake, I entrust this treasure of the Dharma to you, so that they may come to hear such a treasury of the Dharma."
Therefore, Ānanda!
You should cause those sons and daughters of good family who possess pure faith to hear my great treasury of the Dharma-jewel.
Ānanda! If you had not enabled him to hear it, you would have been at fault toward the Tathāgata. Why is this?

Ānanda! If those sons and daughters of good family hear such a great treasury of the Dharma-jewel, some may achieve superior practice, some may give rise to a heart of great love and joy, and some, upon hearing it, may shed tears and have their hair stand on end.

Ānanda! If there are those who, upon hearing this Dharma-gate, weep and their hair stands on end as they recollect the merits of the Buddha, I grant them the prediction that by means of these roots of goodness, they shall all attain nirvāṇa.
The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Scroll Four;
The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Narendrayaśas of India during the Northern Qi Dynasty.
Chapter Thirteen: Planting the Roots of Goodness "Furthermore, Ānanda,

if there are bhikṣus who have received and upheld these Dharma-gates, and there are faithful sons and daughters of good family who come to listen because they delight in hearing the Dharma, yet [the bhikṣus] do not expound them for their sake, such persons are enemies of the Tathāgata."
Why is this? These people are worthy vessels for the Dharma and desire to hear it; because it was not preached to them, they did not hear it.
Because they did not hear it, they have fallen away from their own roots of goodness and have likewise caused others to fall away from their roots of goodness.
Why is this? Because such a person does not know who is fit to be taught and who is unfit to be taught.
"Ānanda!..."
In order to make this meaning clear, I shall provide an analogy.

It is like a merchant who, carrying a great quantity of precious goods, arrives at a vast wilderness on a perilous road; he opens his treasures and spreads them upon the ground, calling out to a band of robbers and saying to them:
"These treasures of mine are rare and difficult to obtain."
"Give me the price, and I shall sell this treasure to you.
Ānanda! At that time, those bandits, in the wilderness, took up their swords and staves, beat the merchants, and seized all their treasures.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Would these merchants be able to spread out their various treasures in the wilderness and call out to the bandits, saying, "Will you buy these goods?"?
Ānanda said: "World-Honored One,
these merchants should not even display their precious goods along the desolate and perilous wilderness paths, much less summon a band of thieves."

In this way, the merchant should securely store his various precious treasures, don armor and take up weapons to protect himself, and thus pass safely through the wilderness; such is what ought to be done.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"Furthermore, there were merchants who also brought various treasures from afar; having arrived at cities, royal capitals, and villages, they opened their treasures and spread them out upon the ground."
Suppose a handsome man comes to purchase their treasures, and these merchants then take up swords and weapons to engage in battle with the purchaser.
Ānanda, what do you think?
"Would these merchants be called clever?
Ānanda replied, "No, Blessed One."
"No, Sugata! World-Honored One!
Those merchants should have spoken thus:"
"These treasures of mine are rare and difficult to obtain; give me the price, and I shall sell them to you.
World-Honored One!
These merchants ought to act in this manner; they should not, after having displayed their various treasures, don armor and take up weapons to resist one another.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

There are bhikṣus who uphold and propagate the treasury of the Dharma-jewels— namely, the sūtras, geyas, gāthās, vyākaraṇas, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas— and yet, although they should be vessels for the Dharma, because [the teaching] was not spoken to them, they have not heard it.”
Because they do not hear [the Dharma], the wholesome mind characterized by faith, aspiration, and delight does not arise;
because it does not arise, they are unable to plant various roots of goodness, cultivate sublime practices, and attain parinirvāṇa.
He preaches to those who are unfit to be vessels for the Dharma; having heard it, they do not give rise to faith, aspiration, or a virtuous mind.
Because these do not arise, they fail to attain liberation. Such persons then engage in slander and disparagement, commit various sinful deeds, and fall into the three evil realms.
Ānanda! It is just like those foolish merchants who open places where treasures should not be opened and do not open places where they ought to be opened;
they are unwilling to give where they should give, yet they force themselves to give where they should not give.

Ānanda! If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith, whose virtuous minds are clear and who delight in hearing the Dharma, and who should be vessels for the Dharma and have come to listen to it—if you fail to speak for those for whom you should speak, or if you forcibly speak to those for whom you should not speak.
Therefore, Ānanda!
If there are those who are capable vessels of the Dharma, possessing deep faith and a longing desire for Nirvāṇa, you should preach it to them.

However, if there are those who are not capable vessels—those who lack faith and a longing desire, who seek out the faults of others, who commit transgressions and evil deeds, and who watch for the failings of others because they wish to oppose the Buddha’s True Eye of the Dharma—you should not preach it to them, as they do not follow it in accordance with the truth.
Why is this? Lest those foolish people, having heard this Dharma, give rise to excessive faults.
Therefore, Ānanda!
One should train in this way:
if there are sons or daughters of good family who are fit vessels for the Dharma and who delight in hearing the Dharma, one should diligently preach it for them;
likewise, all those who listen should also collect their minds and listen with single-minded attention.
Ānanda! If it were thus, both would be able to extensively produce immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) masses of great merit. Ānanda!
"What do you think?
Which is greater: the realm of the earth element or the realm of sentient beings?
Ānanda replied:
“As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, the realm of sentient beings is vast, not so the realm of earth.
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
"So it is, so it is. It is as you have said:
the realm of sentient beings is vast; it is not the element of earth, nor is it the elements of water, fire, and so forth.
Ānanda!"

Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings in the other trichiliocosms—whether they are knowable or unknowable, whether they can be seen or heard or cannot be seen or heard—if all of them were simultaneously to obtain human bodies and become men, and in a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, and a single muhūrta, were all to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; [even so, it would not equal the merit of that person].

Ānanda! Suppose all the earth and soil within immeasurable and boundless world-systems—the limits of which cannot be known—were all ground into fine dust. If all those particles of dust were each to become a human being and each become a man, and if those men, in a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, or a single muhūrta, were all to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha; [even so, it would not equal the merit of one who hears this Dharma].

Ānanda! Suppose that within immeasurable and boundless worlds there are Mount Sumerus, Iron Ring Mountains, Great Iron Ring Mountains, Snowy Mountains, Fragrant Mountains, and other Black Mountains; and even all the medicinal herbs, trees, and forests throughout the trichiliocosm—whether they are discernible or indiscernible, visible and audible or invisible and inaudible—all were to become human beings, all becoming males, and in a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, or a single muhūrta, were all simultaneously to attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.

Ānanda! Suppose those pratyekabuddhas were to have a lifespan extending from the past limit to the future limit—a duration of life remaining in the world that could not be known—yet among all those sentient beings, there would be only one single person who alone could not attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Now, that one person was a great elder, whose lifespan lasted from the past until the end of the future, such that it could not be known;

at that time, the elder also lived for that duration, providing those Pratyekabuddhas with food and drink, clothing, seats, bedding, medicinal decoctions for illness, and all manner of personal requisites and pleasing articles, honoring, respecting, and reverently serving those Pratyekabuddhas with humility.

If, after a Pratyekabuddha has entered parinirvāṇa, one were to erect a stūpa made of the seven precious gems and offer worship with the most excellent offerings among gods and humans—namely, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, various flower garlands, ointments, powdered incense, burning incense, robes, song, dance, vocal music, and instrumental performances—honoring, respecting, and reverently making offerings with humble devotion.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Would that great householder obtain much merit?
Ānanda replied:

"As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, if one were to provide offerings, honor, respect, and reverence to a single pratyekabuddha, the merit obtained would still be vast, immeasurable, incalculable, peerless, limitless, and inconceivable; how much more so for making offerings to as many pratyekabuddhas as there are—honoring, respecting, humbly serving, and providing offerings to them throughout their lifespans or even after they have passed into parinirvāṇa?"
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:

"I now tell you the truth: that Pratyekabuddha, fully endowed with the aggregates of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, accepted the various offerings of that elder."

There was a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who appeared in the world; he did not accept from the householder robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, or medicinal decoctions for the sick, nor did he preach the Dharma.

Nevertheless, the merit obtained by that householder from merely seeing the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha manifesting his ordinary worldly demeanor in the world, is far greater than the merit obtained from making offerings to those Pratyekabuddhas who are fully endowed with morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; it exceeds it by hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of times. The merit obtained by the householder from seeing the Buddha, the Tathāgata, manifesting his ordinary worldly demeanor in the world, cannot be matched.
Why is this? Because the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is fully endowed with immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, and inconceivable great merits. Ānanda!

Even the majestic deportment, merit, and roots of goodness of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, cannot reach their limit; how much less so can one fathom all the immeasurable virtuous merits possessed by the Tathāgata?

Ānanda! If the merit obtained from practicing generosity toward a pratyekabuddha is immeasurable and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya), and the merit obtained from practicing generosity toward a Buddha is likewise immeasurable and limitless, what is the difference between them?
Ānanda! That which is given as a gift is not without distinction. Ānanda!
For example, suppose there is a person who travels to another land for the sake of seeking profit; having obtained that profit, he immediately returns.
Ānanda, the merit obtained from giving to a pratyekabuddha compared to that given to a Buddha-Tathāgata is just like this.
Ānanda! If there were another person who, in the presence of the Buddhas, practiced giving and thereby obtained merit, it would be impossible to provide a simile for it. Why is this?
Ānanda! If one practices giving toward the Buddha, the merit obtained is immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, peerless, matchless, boundless, and inexhaustible.
“Ānanda! Regarding the merit obtained from practicing generosity toward the Buddha, I shall provide you with a simile, for those who possess wisdom attain understanding through similes.”
Ānanda! It is like a painter whose work, though exquisite and fine, still contains some slight flaws that are clumsy and lack dignity;
yet there is another painter whose work is upright and superior even to the former.
In this way, Ānanda!
If one compares the merit obtained from practicing generosity toward a pratyekabuddha with the merit obtained from practicing generosity toward a buddha, it is just like that.
Why is this? Ānanda!

Those pratyekabuddhas receive the name "pratyekabuddha" because of their wisdom; yet all this wisdom of the pratyekabuddhas arises from the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect omniscience) of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, is even more superior than that.
Therefore, Ānanda!

If one were to offer robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, mattresses, and medicinal decoctions for the sick with reverence, respect, humility, and devotion to the Buddha until the end of one's life, would the merit obtained thereby not be great?
Ānanda replied: “So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!”
“World-Honored One, the merit obtained from reverently making offerings to the Buddha for as long as one lives is exceedingly great and immeasurable.

World-Honored One, even the merit obtained from giving rise to a single moment of respectful faith toward the Buddha for as long as one lives is already exceedingly great, immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable; how much more so for someone who, toward the Tathāgata, reverently honors, respects, humbles themselves before, and makes offerings for as long as they live?”
Having spoken these words, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Setting aside the case of one who makes offerings to a single Buddha-Tathāgata with all manner of requisites for pleasure throughout their entire life;
and setting aside the case of one who makes offerings to two, three, four, five, or even ten Buddhas..."
Twenty, thirty, or even up to a hundred Buddhas, a thousand Buddhas, a hundred thousand Buddhas,
ten million Buddhas, a hundred billion Buddhas, a thousand billion Buddhas, a hundred thousand billion Buddhas,
ten billion nayutas, a hundred billion nayutas, a thousand billion nayutas, a hundred thousand billion nayutas, and even throughout...
Filling Jambudvīpa with Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas— extending throughout the four continents, a thousand-world system, a two-thousand-world system,
and a three-thousand great thousand-world system, including therein ten billion suns and moons,
ten billion Sumeru mountains, ten billion Cakravāḍa mountain ranges, ten billion great oceans, and ten billion Jambudvīpas.
One billion Purvavidehas, one billion Uttarakurus, one billion Aparagodānīyas,
eighty thousand islands and their surrounding dependencies, one billion sets of four continents,
one billion Cāturmahārājika heavens, one billion Trāyastriṃśa heavens, one billion Yāma heavens, and one billion Tuṣita heavens.
The Yāma Heaven, ten billion Nirmāṇarati Heavens, ten billion Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heavens,
ten billion Brahmā Heavens, up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven— this is called a trichiliocosm—
were all completely filled with Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, just like a field of sugarcane.
Whether it be forests of bamboo, reeds, khadira trees, or kāśa trees,
the lifespans of those Tathāgatas are as long as the kalpas of the sands of the Ganges River.

At that time, there was an elder whose lifespan remained in the world for an equally long duration; throughout his entire life, he reverently, respectfully, and humbly made offerings to those Tathāgatas, providing them with clothing, food and drink, seats, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for illness and debility.

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one were to erect a stūpa made of the seven precious gems and honor, revere, and venerate it with humility, using celestial banners and streamers, various exquisite jeweled canopies, all kinds of incense and flowers, ointments, powdered incense, all manner of floral garlands, various wonderful lotuses—utpala, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka—as well as all forms of song and dance and various musical instruments; that is, by means of all such articles of pleasure.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Would the merit obtained by that great householder be much?"
Ānanda replied: “So it is, Blessed One! So it is, Sugata!”

The merit obtained by that great householder from making offerings of various delicacies and foods to a single Tathāgata is already immeasurable and incalculable; how much more so when, for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, one provides offerings, shows reverence, respect, and humility toward all Buddhas, and after those Buddhas have passed into extinction, erects stupas made of the seven precious gems and makes various offerings to them?
"The merit thus obtained is beyond comparison.
Having spoken these words, the Buddha told Ānanda: "I now tell you the truth:

if that elder, throughout the lifespans of those Buddhas, were to revere, respect, humble himself before, and make offerings to them; and if, after those Buddhas had passed into parinirvāṇa, he were to erect stūpas of the seven treasures and make all kinds of supreme and wondrous offerings to them—the merit obtained from this would be even greater."
Ānanda! If there are good men or good women who, when the Tathāgatas analytically expound the path to enlightenment, believe, understand, and aspire to it, possessing deep faith such that they think:
"The Dharma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha are those who have resolved their minds and practice well."

"Ānanda, he has faith and understanding that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all are suffering, all are empty, all dharmas are without self, and that they culminate in the tranquility of nirvāṇa."
The merit obtained through such faith and understanding is even more superior than the former. Ānanda!

If there were another person who, with faith and understanding, [receives] this treasury of the Dharma jewels and in turn explains it to others, the merit they obtain would be as vast, as immeasurable, as incalculable (asaṃkhyeya), as inconceivable, as peerless, and as limitless as this.
Why is this? Ānanda!

Such a Dharma-treasure, the unsurpassed treasury of the Dharma, is good in the beginning, middle, and end. If one were to compare the merit obtained from practicing such generosity to this treasury of the Dharma, it would be like a mere blade of grass; you should know it thus.
Why is this? Ānanda!
Such giving as this is mundane, with outflows, and is a dharma of birth and death.

Ānanda! This treasury of Dharma, which I have accumulated over immeasurable asaṃkhyeya billions of nayutas of kalpas, exists for the purpose of severing birth and death, and for the sake of transcending all various forms of nutriment and cyclic existence.
Ānanda! If there are sentient beings who hear this treasury of the Dharma, they will attain liberation from the arising of dharmas;
they will even attain liberation from the dharmas of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
Ānanda! It is with reference to this meaning that I have made this statement: there are two kinds of people who obtain great merit;
first, those who preach with a diligent mind, and second, those who listen with a sincere and focused mind.
Having spoken these words, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who possess profound faith, practice in accordance with reality by discerning all phenomena, and who—with faith, understanding, and aspiration—believe that the Dharma is well-expounded and that the Saṃgha consists of those who have resolved their minds to practice well; and who, through faith and understanding, realize that all conditioned formations are impermanent, whether they be suffering or empty, and that all phenomena are without self, and that Nirvāṇa is quiescent extinction.”
“If one thus reflects well and possesses profound, correct mindfulness, how much merit will they obtain?
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!

Furthermore, if there are people who know only that the Dharma is well-expounded and that the Saṅgha are those who have resolved their minds to practice well, such sons and daughters of good family, through profound and correct reflection, focus their minds and listen attentively; having heard the Dharma, they engage in profound and correct reflection for even as long as a finger-snap:
"The Dharma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha are those who have resolved their minds to practice well."
"The merit obtained by such a person would be immeasurable and boundless.

How much more so for a son or daughter of good family who, through profound and correct reflection, restrains the mind and listens with single-minded devotion; and having heard the Dharma, practices it as it truly is for even the duration of a finger-snap, understanding that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all are suffering, all are empty, all dharmas are selfless, and that there is the tranquility of Nirvana?"

Ānanda! Suppose that within all the realms of sentient beings across immeasurable and boundless worlds, every single being were simultaneously to obtain a human body in a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, or a single muhūrta;
and having obtained those human bodies, they were simultaneously to attain equal and perfect enlightenment in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, or a single muhūrta.
The lifespans of those Tathāgatas, even from the beginningless past, cannot be known; it is likewise for the future. Ānanda!

Suppose among all these sentient beings there were only one person who did not attain perfect awakening in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; yet that single person would be a great elder, and his lifespan too, from the beginningless past, could not be known, and it would be likewise for the future.

At that time, the elder, for as long as he lived, reverently honored, respected, humbled himself before, and made offerings to those Tathāgatas, providing them with all manner of articles of pleasure, clothing, food and drink, seats, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for illness and debility.

After those Tathāgatas have entered parinirvāṇa, one shall erect stūpas made of the seven precious substances; having erected these stūpas, one shall reverently, respectfully, and humbly make offerings with jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, all kinds of flower garlands, ointments, and powdered incense—whatever exists in the world.
Ānanda! What do you think?
Is the merit obtained by that householder at that time not indeed great?
Ānanda said:
