"If that elder were to reverently honor, respect, humble himself before, and make offerings to a single Tathāgata Buddha, the merit he would obtain would be exceedingly great, immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, peerless, and limitless; how much more so if he were to do so toward all Buddhas throughout their entire lifespans?"
"The merit thus obtained is inconceivable.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
It is so, it is so; it is just as you have said. The merit obtained by this householder is inconceivable.
Therefore, Ānanda, I now tell you the truth:

if that householder were to revere, honor, humble himself before, and make offerings to those Buddhas for the duration of their entire lifespans, the merit he would thereby obtain—[would be even greater than what he has already gained].

Furthermore, if there is another person who, through profound and correct reflection, focuses the mind to listen attentively, and having heard the Dharma, for even as long as a finger-snap, develops faith, understanding, and aspiration—believing that the Dharma is well-expounded and that the Saṅgha are those who have resolved to practice correctly—and who believes and understands that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, empty, and that all dharmas are without self, and that there is the quiescent Nirvāṇa; the merit obtained by such a person cannot be known through any analogy.
Ānanda! As I have previously stated, there are two kinds of people who obtain immense merit: first, those who explain with a sincere heart; second, those who listen with single-minded diligence.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"For the sake of two purposes, One should listen to what the Buddha teaches:
The exhaustion of all taints and conditioned formations, And approaching the noble ones to achieve Bodhi."
"If there is one who preaches the Dharma, and one who listens to the Buddha’s true Dharma,
both shall obtain abundant merit and be able to raise the banners of the sages.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
“There are two kinds of people who engage in a great battle and dispute with Māra Pāpīyān. Who are these two?
First, those who preach with a sincere heart; second, those who listen with single-minded diligence.”
Why is this? Ānanda!
That which brings such a holy life (brahmacarya) to fulfillment consists of virtuous friends and virtuous companions, through whom the stream of wholesome mind flows.
Why is this? Ānanda!

If there are sentient beings who encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), having encountered such a friend, they attain liberation from birth, and even attain liberation from the phenomena of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
Ānanda! Regarding this matter, I have previously told all the śrāvakas that there are two causes and conditions by which right view can arise:
first, hearing the Dharma from others; second, correct internal reflection.
Those who hear it from others should know that they hear it from the Buddha; those who engage in internal right reflection also know it through the Buddha.
Why is this? Ānanda!
Just as ordinary worldlings lacked internal right reflection on their own before the Buddha appeared in the world,
once the Buddha had appeared in the world, he taught ordinary worldlings to engage in such practice.
"Ānanda! It is because I contemplate this meaning that I have made this statement: 'Internal right reflection also arises from the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Excellent, O sublime man! By beholding you, all wisdom increases;
for those who sever their doubts, you cause ordinary beings to attain clear insight.
Seeing a noble one brings joy, and dwelling together with them also brings joy.”
"I do not see any ordinary fools who possess constant happiness.
Therefore, Ānanda, for this purpose I have taught according to what is appropriate:
that those whose holy life is fulfilled—namely, spiritual friends and virtuous companions—are able to give rise to wholesome states of mind, which flow on in continuous succession.
Why is this? Ānanda!
If there are sentient beings who encounter a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they will give rise to a wholesome mind.
Once a wholesome mind has arisen, the mind attains faith;
once the mind has attained faith, all that one does is wholesome;
once what one does is wholesome, one then attains wholesome dharmas.
Having attained wholesome qualities, one dwells securely in those wholesome qualities;

having so dwelt, one develops profound reverence for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and likewise profound reverence for the Dharma and the Saṅgha. One shall then attain the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones, the precepts of mastery, the precepts praised by the wise, and the precepts that lead toward Nirvāṇa.

Ānanda! Just as when clouds send down rain, the small pools are filled; once the small pools are filled, the large pools are filled; once the large pools are filled, the small rivers are filled; once the small rivers are filled, the great rivers are filled; and once the great rivers are filled, the great ocean is filled.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who, having heard the Buddhas speak in their presence, attain the power of roots of goodness;
having attained these roots of goodness, they draw near to spiritual friends.
Having approached virtuous spiritual friends, one obtains virtuous companions;
having obtained virtuous companions, one obtains a virtuous stream;
having obtained a virtuous stream, one attains the most excellent goodness.
Having attained the most excellent goodness, one attains a virtuous mind;

having attained a virtuous mind, one proceeds until—acting in accordance with the Dharma, conforming to the Dharma—one brings the cultivation of the awakened mind to its ultimate transformation, its ultimate stainlessness, its ultimate holy life, and its ultimate finality.
“Ānanda! Observe how all these external things grow simultaneously, and when their flowers and fruits reach maturity, there is no failure or loss.
How much more so for the wholesome deeds you yourselves perform—how could they ever fail or be lost?”
If there were any violation or failure [in this regard], such a thing is impossible. Therefore, Ānanda!
You all should practice wholesome conduct; there is no sentient being who practices wholesome conduct and yet fails to obtain its fruit, nor is there any who violates it.
Ānanda! I too have practiced all wholesome deeds, without any transgression or failure. Ānanda!
"When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, there was no failure or loss regarding the karmic fruits obtained from all the virtuous merits I cultivated. Ānanda! "

Observe, O son, how the road traversed by the Tathāgata becomes level and even, with all its hills, mounds, pits, and depressions; how latrines and foul places become pure, fragrant, and clean; how stumps, thorns, thickets, forests, and weeds—though once filthy and obstructive—are suppressed and rendered excellent; and how the tree spirits manifest their forms, bowing low in prostration. All sentient beings within the cities and along the streets follow the Tathāgata as he proceeds, yet once the Tathāgata has passed, everything returns to its former state.

Ānanda! Observe how the Tathāgata, in the past, before all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, spiritual friends, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, preceptors, parents, elders, seniors, śramaṇas, and brahmins, bowed his head in prostration; thereby he has obtained such a most supreme karmic fruit: that when all external objects behold the Buddhas, those that ought to bow their heads immediately bow, the high are made low, the low are made high, and all places, whether high or low, become entirely level and even.

“Ānanda! Observe all foolish worldlings who do not cultivate reverence toward their elders and seniors, nor do they pay them homage; they are arrogant and self-reliant, harmed by pride and entangled by pride.”
“Ānanda! Behold the Tathāgata’s hands and feet with their webbed fingers and toes; all have been obtained through the practice of wholesome deeds. Ānanda!”

Observe how the Tathāgata originally cultivated virtuous conduct—generosity, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation—and through these virtuous deeds gathered and protected sentient beings without making distinctions such as, "This is my father," "This is my mother," "my brother," "my sister," "my relative," or "my good friend."
Ānanda! Toward all sentient beings, I am of a single flavor and equal, my mind free from discrimination. Ānanda!

Throughout the long, distant past, there has been no sentient being whom I have not gathered through giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation. In this way, I have sustained and protected foolish worldlings; yet they do not realize that, by virtue of their own roots of goodness and the causes and conditions of their merit, they receive various retributions throughout the beginningless limits of birth and death.
Ānanda! The merit and happiness I obtain from bestowing roots of goodness upon sentient beings are greater than the karmic fruits I obtain from practicing various wholesome deeds myself. Ānanda!
All the articles of pleasure existing in all worlds are impermanent; they are phenomena subject to change, for such articles of pleasure are impermanent.

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I did so to bring ordinary and ignorant beings to maturity in the Buddha-way, enabling them to attain the unconditioned, noble, and untainted bliss—this untainted bliss is permanent and unchanging, never again to be destroyed.
Therefore, Ānanda, one should cultivate all activities with such noble wisdom; this cultivation of all activities with such noble wisdom is called right action.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
In the past, I too cultivated various wholesome deeds by means of this noble wisdom.
Ānanda! I shall further explain other wholesome practices as well.

If there are sentient beings who, for the sake of nirvāṇa, even give rise to the thought of cultivating a small root of goodness and plant various seeds—such as hearing the Tathāgata preach the various sublime dharmas and deeply understanding their meaning and intent, or recollecting the Tathāgata with a heart of love and reverence, shedding tears, heaving long sighs, or having their hair stand on end—it is impossible that they should fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts;
it is also impossible that they should not attain ultimate realization in bodhi.
Ānanda! Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, recollecting the Tathāgata and awakening to the Dharma, shed tears, have their hair stand on end, and heave sighs. Ānanda!
Do not view this otherwise; it is impossible for those sentient beings to fall into the evil realms—the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.
Therefore, Ānanda! Do not be negligent;
you should diligently apply skillful means to cultivate all wholesome karmas.
“Ānanda! [he said.]
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have realized enlightenment through heedfulness, and the factors conducive to the path are likewise attained through heedfulness. Ānanda!
If there are those who properly receive the teachings, who seek benefit, who seek peace and happiness, and who seek compassion, they should act in this way, giving rise to a heart of pity and mercy.

"What ought to be done has already been completed by me; you all should now likewise do it, so that this true path may not be severed, and furthermore, so that the Buddha’s eye of the True Dharma does not vanish."
Ānanda! You should cause the eye of the Buddha’s Dharma to endure for a long time in this way, widely circulating and disseminating it among humans and devas. Ānanda!
"I now entrust this treasury of the true Dharma to you; do not allow it to perish. You should act in this manner; this is my teaching. Chapter 14:
The Chapter on Instruction The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on Instruction At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
How shall I now practice the Dharma-eye?
If I practice the Buddha’s true Dharma-eye, how can it remain long-lasting and be widely disseminated among devas and humans?
"Bhagavān!
How shall I further compile the Eye of the Dharma?
How shall I proclaim it?"
Having spoken these words, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"After my parinirvāṇa, when the assembly of great virtuous bhikṣus gathers to compile the Dharma and Vinaya, that great virtuous Mahākāśyapa shall be their foremost leader."
Ānanda! At that time, the assembly of those great virtuous bhikṣus shall ask thus:
"In what place did the World-Honored One speak the Mahāpadeśa?"
In what place was the Mahānidāna spoken?
In what place was the Mahāsannipāta-dharma spoken?
In what place were the five sets of three dharmas spoken?
From where do the various devas come to inquire?
From where does Śakra, Lord of Devas, come to inquire?
From where have the various devas descended?
"In what place was the Brahmajāla Sūtra preached?
In this manner, those bhikṣus will further question you:
"Ānanda!..."
In what place did the Buddha preach the Sūtras?
In what place did he preach the Geyas?
In what place did he preach the Vyākaraṇas?
Wherein are the gāthās spoken?
Wherein are the udānas spoken?
Wherein are the nidānas spoken?
In what place is the Itivṛttaka taught?
In what place is the Jātaka taught?
In what place is the Vaipulya taught?
In what place is the *avadāna* taught?
In what place is the *apadāna* taught?
In what place is the *upadeśa* taught?
Ānanda! In what place did the Buddha preach the Śrāvaka-piṭaka?
In what place did the Buddha preach the Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka?
"In what place did the Buddha teach the Bodhisattva-piṭaka? "Ānanda!
When that bhikṣu has asked this, you should answer him as follows:"
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was at the Bodhi tree in the kingdom of Magadha, having newly attained perfect enlightenment;
thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was in the city of Gayā;
thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in the kingdom of Magadha, at the place where he practiced austerities beneath the Ajapāla-nigrodha tree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at the Abode of the Sages;
thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was on Mount Vipula.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying on Mount Vaideha in the kingdom of Magadha;
thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was at the Great Black Square Stone on Mount Ṛṣigiri near Rājagṛha;
thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Āmra Grove in the city of Vaiśālī.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at the Mahāvana Monastery on the upper story of the lecture hall by the Markaṭahrada Lake in Vaiśālī;
thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was staying at the Kakutthā Lake in the city of Campā.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was at Gayā, on the summit of Mount Gayā;
thus have I heard.
At one time the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu, the residence of the Śākyas, in the Nyagrodha Park;
thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was staying at Pāṭaliputra, in the Kukkuṭa Park.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying in the city of Mathurā, in the Piṇḍavana forest;
thus have I heard:
"At one time the Buddha was staying between the twin śāla trees on the banks of the Ārīṭaka River at Kuśinagara, in the birthplace of the Mallas. 'Ānanda!'"

In this sequential manner, wherever the Buddha has taught the Dharma and wherever great assemblies have gathered, he has expounded it according to the appropriate time, according to the phrasing and meaning, according to the causes and conditions, and according to the origins of the questions and answers;
according to the persons addressed and the matters at hand, he has preached in various ways through the sequence of names, phrases, and meanings, desiring to analyze and manifest his wisdom;
following those threads, causes, and conditions, he has extensively explained the excellent meaning and excellent phrasing for the sake of others.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the entire great assembly was filled with immense joy; they received it upon their heads and practiced it accordingly. "Ānanda!
You should thus collect the Eye of the Dharma, distinguishing and explaining in detail these various words spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha: 'Thus have I heard.'"
When this was said, the great earth shook in six ways with extreme violence; it was most terrifying, causing the hair on one's body to stand on end.

At that moment, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, manifesting eighteen signs: the east rose and the west sank; the west rose and the east sank; the south rose and the north sank; the north rose and the south sank; the center rose and the periphery sank; and the periphery rose and the center sank.

The eighteen signs are: shaking, shaking everywhere, shaking equally everywhere; leaping, leaping everywhere, leaping equally everywhere; quaking, quaking everywhere, quaking equally everywhere; roaring, roaring everywhere, roaring equally everywhere; rising, rising everywhere, rising equally everywhere; awakening, awakening everywhere, awakening equally everywhere.

At that time, immeasurable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, humans, non-humans, and others wept with streaming tears and spoke these words: “Bhagavān!
Nirvāṇa is too soon! Sugata,
Nirvāṇa is too soon!
"The Eye of the World has vanished too soon; the world has become blind and sightless too soon.
The Venerable Ānanda, weeping with streaming tears, also spoke these words: "Bhagavān!..."
Nirvāṇa is too soon! Sugata,
Nirvāṇa is too soon!
"The Eye of the World has vanished too soon; the world has become blind and sightless too soon; the Guide of the World has vanished too soon.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Do not grieve or lament."

All conditioned phenomena—phenomena that arise, phenomena that exist, phenomena that are conceptualized, phenomena that are cognized, phenomena produced by causes and conditions, and phenomena subject to disintegration—it is impossible for them not to disintegrate.

Ānanda! Throughout the long night, you have served the Tathāgata with loving-kindness and filial piety through body, speech, and mind, providing immeasurable peace and happiness; your mind has been without duality, free from anger, free from resentment, and free from enmity or malice.
Ānanda! By means of this, you shall attain great supernormal powers and great merit, vast and immeasurable, like nectar, the supreme nectar, reaching the very limit of nectar.
Therefore, Ānanda!
You too should likewise honor and make offerings to the holy life with body, speech, and mind; you should train yourself just as I have done.
Why is this? Ānanda!

After my parinirvāṇa, in the future age when the Dharma is about to perish—during the final five hundred years—the factions that uphold the precepts and the factions of the True Dharma will be on the verge of total extinction.

Ānanda! When there is a proliferation of those who break the precepts and form factions of unrighteousness, when they slander the True Dharma, and when the lifespan of sentient beings is shortened—at that time of the ruin of sentient beings, the destruction of the Dharma, and the degeneration of the Saṅgha of bhikṣus—[this will occur].
At that time, amidst such alarm, dread, and fear,
there will be bhikṣus who do not cultivate the body, do not cultivate the mind, do not cultivate ethical discipline, and do not cultivate wisdom.
Those who do not cultivate the body, ethical discipline, mind, and wisdom will become greedily attached to the six sense bases.

What are the six? First, attachment to alms bowls; second, attachment to robes; third, attachment to food; fourth, attachment to beds and seats; fifth, attachment to dwellings; and sixth, attachment to medicinal decoctions due to the causes and conditions of illness and debility.

Because they greedily crave excellent robes and alms bowls, as well as the finest varieties of medicinal elixirs, they further engage in mutual strife and litigious disputes, even escalating to the official courts; their mouths are like swords and blades as they slander one another, harboring mutual hatred and envy.

In this way, on account of robes, alms bowls, food and drink, bedding and seats, dwellings, and medicinal requisites, they harbor mutual hatred and jealousy; their minds are not matured, and they face one another with turbid hearts.
Therefore, Ānanda!
You should properly provide for those living the holy life (brahmacārin) with kindness of body, speech, and mind, and offer them complete support.

Whether you see or hear of those living the holy life, whether their conduct is coarse or subtle, whether they are faithful or practicing, you must not cause them any disturbance or agitation; you should train yourself in this way.
Why is this? Ānanda!

At that time, there will be extreme terror—the turbidity of life, the turbidity of the eon, the turbidity of sentient beings, the turbidity of views, and the turbidity of afflictions. At that time, worldly people will undergo extreme suffering; they will be struck by suffering, tormented by suffering, afflicted by extreme famine, afflicted by extreme pestilence, troubled by bandits, beset by droughts and floods, and harassed by various kinds of insects and vermin.

“Ānanda! At that time, although those brahmins, householders, and lay devotees were thus afflicted by suffering and tormented by suffering, they still possessed pure faith, reverence, and respect for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and they repeatedly gave rise to a complete and profound faith.”

By virtue of his faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, he also develops deep faith in even a single bhikṣu; he practices generosity, performs various meritorious deeds, upholds the prohibitive precepts, recites and masters the teachings, and explains them to others.

There are those who, having heard and received the Dharma, give rise to love and reverence in their hearts; filled with joy and exultation, they practice according to the Dharma and plant various roots of goodness. By virtue of these roots of goodness, when their bodies perish and their lives end, they attain rebirth in the happy realms—among the devas and humans.

“Ānanda! Observe these evil bhikṣus: having left home out of faith to enter the homeless life, once they have become renunciants, they fall into the three evil realms due to attachment to robes and bowls through six causes and conditions;
whereas laypeople, though tormented by suffering, still give rise to respectful faith, and by means of the roots of goodness born of that faith, attain birth in the good realms.”
Therefore, Ānanda, you should maintain proper restraint of the body, restraint of speech, and restraint of the mind, and you should form this thought:
"May I quickly attain fullness of reverent faith; may I attain fullness of an upright and sincere heart; may my body and mind be endowed with wholesome reflection."
Why is this? Ānanda! There are five kinds of faults in unwholesome reflection regarding the actions of body, speech, and mind.
What are the five? First, false speech;
second, divisive speech; third, frivolous speech; fourth, covetousness; and fifth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, falling into the three evil realms and being born in hell.
“Ānanda! One who practices right reflection shall obtain five kinds of meritorious benefits. What are these five?

First, refraining from false speech; second, refraining from divisive speech; third, refraining from frivolous speech; fourth, refraining from covetousness; fifth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, one will attain rebirth in a good destination—among the gods or humans.
"Furthermore, Ānanda!
If a person engages in quarreling, reviling, litigation, and contentious opposition, such that their mind is neither pliant nor gentle and their turbid mind is corrupted, there are five faults.

First, false speech; second, divisive speech; third, failing to give rise to reverence and faith toward those who uphold the precepts; fourth, dwelling with a mind of malice and sorrowful suffering day and night; and fifth, upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, falling into the three evil realms and being born within the hells.
“Ānanda! If there is another person whose mind dwells in loving-kindness and compassion, they shall obtain eleven kinds of meritorious benefits.
What are these eleven?

First, one obtains tranquility in sleep and joy upon awakening; second, one does not see evil dreams; third, humans and non-humans hold one dear; fourth, one is protected by the devas; fifth, poisons cannot harm one; sixth, blades and arrows do not wound one; seventh, fire does not burn one; eighth, water does not drown one; ninth, one constantly obtains fine clothing, delicacies, food and drink, seats, bedding, and medicinal decoctions for illness; tenth, one attains the qualities of a superior person; eleventh, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in the Brahma Heaven.
"Ānanda! By abiding in a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, one attains these eleven kinds of meritorious benefits. Therefore, Ānanda!"
Whether I am present now or have passed into parinirvāṇa, you should take the Dharma as your lamp and the Dharma as your refuge; do not seek another lamp, and do not seek another refuge. Ānanda!
What is meant by a bhikṣu who is a lamp unto himself, a refuge unto himself, seeking no other lamp and seeking no other refuge? Ānanda,
it is when a bhikṣu contemplates the body internally, observing the body with diligence and vigor, with mindfulness focused and the mind one-pointed, removing worldly greed and sorrow.

In this way, Ānanda, one contemplates the internal body, observing the body as it is; one contemplates internal feelings, the internal mind, and internal phenomena—exerting diligent energy, maintaining mindfulness with a single-pointed mind, and removing worldly greed and sorrow.
This is what it means for a bhikṣu to have the Dharma as his own lamp and the Dharma as his refuge, seeking no other lamp and seeking no other refuge.
Therefore, Ānanda!
I am your guide; that which was to be done by the śrāvakas has been fully accomplished by me. You should now act in this manner.

This is my teaching: you should, in forest retreats, among cemeteries, at the foot of trees, in empty huts, or in the open air, single-mindedly and diligently cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, contemplating the cessation of the root of suffering, and be careful not to be negligent.
If you are negligent, you will surely feel grief and regret later.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"I have already taught the Right Path, And extracted the arrows of ignorance;
You should now diligently cultivate The Dharma taught by all Buddhas."
To purify all views, there is no path other than this;
by practicing it, one attains liberation and is able to sever the bonds of all Māras.
If one can practice this conduct as taught by the Buddha, [one shall attain the goal].
"One can transcend all suffering and fulfill the vows of all Buddhas.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had finished preaching this sutra, the Venerable Ānanda, the bhikṣus, the great assembly who had gathered, as well as the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and all those in the world, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were moved by a mixture of sorrow and joy. They raised their hands and struck their heads, beat their breasts and wailed, weeping with streaming tears, before receiving and upholding the teaching with the highest reverence.
The Mahākaruṇā Sūtra, Scroll Five
